A key obstacle in kidney transplants arises from the incompatibility between donors and patients, which has been exacerbated by the growing scarcity of kidney donors. Desensitization techniques were developed to overcome the immunological difficulties. Patients receiving incompatible transplants face a higher risk of transplant rejection, infections, and cancer, and are more likely to lose their transplants. We aim to find the optimal acceptance criteria for end-stage kidney patients by potentially receiving incompatible kidneys. A Markov Decision Process model is introduced, which accounts for the level of incompatibility as a key factor, making it a more complex problem to solve, but with suitable conditions, it is possible to establish control limit policies that can be easily applied. Our study uses numerical examples to demonstrate how the optimal policy behaves under different levels of incompatibility, and highlights the significance of taking incompatibility into consideration in decision-making, especially when desensitization treatments are available. Furthermore, we outline the potential advancements in treating desensitization treatments as part of learning, rejection treatment, and donor retention, which is a significant area for future research. Overall, our study provides insights into the strategic decision-making required for kidney transplants with incompatible donors and patients. From a mathematical perspective, our research expands the applications of MDP models, particularly in scenarios with non-analytical values for state and action costs. Our approach involves developing a new MDP cost formulation that can be useful in other contexts, such as electricity pricing, where the cost of control actions varies significantly depending on the system state. Our approach also implies that there are more efficient policy evaluation algorithms available, which can be utilized in the simulation environment we developed. Our research demonstrates the value of considering incompatibility in decision-making, which is particularly important in scenarios with desensitization treatments, rejection treatment, and donor retention, which involve complex trade-offs between short-term and long-term costs. Our approach can be expanded further by incorporating additional state dimensions, such as time, and nonlinear relationships between state and action costs, which would require the development of new algorithmic solutions. Our approach can be used in other contexts, such as electricity pricing, which involves time-dependent state and action costs. This paper undertakes a comprehensive mathematical examination of the word2vec model, particularly in its implementation with the Skip-gram learning method. We investigate how NLP embeddings, now widely applied, are impacted by the distribution of terms within a given corpus. A mathematical framework is employed to elucidate the implicit structural assumptions of the model, revealing its reliance on Markovian assumptions that provide a clear theoretical understanding of how embeddings are generated and capture the essence of frequentist synonyms. We also develop generative models and conduct explicit analyses of commonly used loss functions. To further illustrate the limitations of these models, we create synthetic corpora with varying levels of complexity, demonstrating the ability (or inability) of word2vec to effectively learn these structures. We also empirically assess the capabilities of these models using a substantial financial news dataset covering 12 years and spanning 42 million articles, relying on the Loughran-McDonald Sentiment Word Lists. Our results show that these models are prone to confusing antonyms as frequentist synonyms and mixing terms with opposing polarities. Notably, our research also uncovers the non-stationarity of financial corpora, revealing time-varying patterns in cosine similarity among polarized words or company names. This research introduces a new method to model the interaction of fluids with changing phases, combining level-set and embedded boundary techniques. By leveraging the strengths of these approaches, we've developed a numerical strategy utilizing Cartesian grids to efficiently handle complex boundary transformations and high-resolution interface representation. This method enables a second-order conservative numerical scheme and has been effectively applied to solve various problems, including Stefan problems, dendrite growth, and Rayleigh--B\'enard instabilities, even in the presence of melting boundaries. Furthermore, we've developed a novel algorithm to treat the freezing of complex geometries and have incorporated this method into an open-source code, which we use to validate our approach against existing studies and experimental data. By successfully modeling a range of scenarios with shifting boundaries and comparing the results with other studies, we demonstrate the versatility and accuracy of this new method. This approach shows particular promise for modeling fluid interactions with changing phases in more complex settings, such as melting galaxies and the formation of planetary cores. This research is an extension of a previous study, where we applied a similar approach to model the movement of fluids within changing phases in the presence of gravity, with applications to planetary core formation. This new work expands upon that foundation by improving the algorithm for handling the freezing of complex boundaries and adding additional problem solving capabilities. In multiagent learning settings beyond finding equilibria, learning rationalizable behavior that steers clear of dominated actions is another key goal. However, existing algorithms in the general multiplayer games scenario require an exponentially large number of samples relative to the number of players to determine rationalizable equilibria when working under bandit feedback. This research develops an initial suite of efficient algorithms to learn both Coarse Correlated Equilibria (CCE) and Correlated Equilibria (CE) that achieve polynomial sample complexities in line with problem parameters including the number of players. It also includes an enhanced approach for identifying a rationalizable action profile with a significantly improved sample requirement, exceeding the current benchmark established in 2021. Our innovative solutions involve the integration of multiple cutting-edge techniques that concurrently ensure the rationalizability and absence of (swap-)regret through correlated exploration and dynamic learning rate adjustments, offering potential value as standalone contributions. Moreover, our results are complemented by a sample complexity lower bound, underscoring the precision of the devised guarantees. This research and its findings are relevant to a broader context of learning from feedback in multiagent settings. Integrating diverse datasets, stemming from data and theoretical sources, is a prerequisite for accurately fitting probability density functions. While aligning the format of experimental data is a straightforward process, reconciling disparate theoretical predictions is a more complex task. Given the numerous contributors to different physical processes, with various inputs and outputs, incorporating the predictions requires significant integration efforts. Furthermore, since processes are often measured across a wide range of scales, evolution equations such as DGLAP need to be applied to PDF candidates or already precomputed in the outputs, necessitating a unified framework that can automate this process for the benefit of research groups working on PDF fitting and potential phenomenological studies. To address this challenge, we present a versatile tool called `pdf4lhc` that can collectively incorporate a broad range of PDF candidates, with support for major sets of LHC-compatible PDFs, along with an integrated toolkit for managing the application of evolution equations to various inputs and outputs, and the corresponding `Python` classes and documentation to ensure accessibility for future developments. Additionally, we provide an evaluation of the impact of PDF model density on anomalous scaling violations in deep inelastic scattering cross-section data, demonstrating the critical importance of correctly integrated PDFs for accurate predictions. Ultimately, the `pdf4lhc` tool is an essential contribution to the PDF fitting community, with far-reaching implications for phenomenological studies across the entire spectrum of particle interactions. The associated PDF sets, along with `pdf4lhc` itself, are available for download at the CERN PDF lattice website, alongside instructions for use and future development opportunities. The impact of PDF model density on the production of top-quark pairs in proton-proton collisions is particularly notable, with variations in the top-quark cross-section reaching up to 10% among different PDF candidates, highlighting the need for rigorous PDF fitting and inclusion of relevant corrections in potential phenomenological studies. The underlying research has been validated through extensive testing within standardized workflows used in high-energy physics, along with simulations of actual production environments, to ensure the efficacy of the proposed solution in real-world applications. The underlying code of the `pdf4lhc` tool is an open-source contribution to the global scientific community, with the associated PDF sets released under the most liberal free licenses available, to facilitate widespread adoption and future development of the technology. The underlying challenge, the developed solution, and the associated findings are all relevant to ongoing and future PDF fitting efforts within the particle physics community, along with potential applications in other domains involving fit parameter estimation. We introduce MG-GLAM, a computational tool developed to rapidly create comprehensive N-body simulations for various cosmological theories, specifically modified gravity models. This program builds upon the existing GLAM code and incorporates an advanced multigrid method to solve the non-linear equations characteristic of modified gravity theories, resulting in highly efficient simulations. For $f(R)$ gravity, MG-GLAM includes multiple variations that mimic distinct behaviors of these models and offers tailored algorithms to maintain speed and precision. The code excels at producing a broad spectrum of modified gravity simulations and offers significant computational benefits, outperforming existing N-body simulations by a factor of over a hundred while yielding accurate results for key cosmological metrics. MG-GLAM is suited for creating large sets of modified gravity simulations that can be utilized in mock galaxy catalogues and emulators for ongoing and future galaxy surveys. This package is designed to streamline the process of testing galaxy evolution through simulations of the given type, allowing for a comprehensive examination of modified gravity theories across various scales and lengths of time. The code is part of a larger project that includes tools for creating mock galaxy catalogues and emulators based on multiple cosmological theories. This work is particularly relevant to ongoing and future galaxy surveys, such as DESI, Euclid, and LSST, that require the simulation of galaxy evolution on large scales over extended periods of time. MG-GLAM enables the efficient generation of cosmological simulations for an inclusive range of modified gravity models and emerges as a crucial resource for accurately testing these types of theories through galaxy evolution simulations. This project is an element of a larger research initiative that also comprises a standalone code, _halglam_, designed to generate N-body simulations of a specific type of modified gravity, $f(R)$ gravity, and a code, _halglam emulator_, utilized to create mock galaxy catalogues and emulators based on those simulations. Both of these codes are part of the broader project mentioned above. Miller and Sheffield introduced the concept of an imaginary surface as a pairing of subdomains of the complex plane and associated Gaussian free fields under conformal equivalence. Specifically, they considered the relationship between these pairings and chordal Schramm-Loewner evolution. This paper develops Gaussian free field-valued processes in the upper half-plane and the first orthant of the complex plane, establishing their connection to multiple SLE evolving in time on these domains. We demonstrate that such connections can be made locally by driving multiple SLE with the Dyson model on the real line and the Bru-Wishart process on the positive reals, respectively. Ultimately, these pairings yield domains that evolve in time and associated Gaussian free fields. We refer to these as multiple time multiple SLE with branching (mtmsl\eb) on these domains. This process generates branching boundary segments at points where the time parameter reaches zero, evolving according to a multi-time Karlin-McGregor process. We discover that mtmsl\eb on the upper half-plane generates the Dolgopolov boundary loop process, whereas mtmsl\eb on the first orthant gives rise to a loop ensemble whose statistics match those described by the M sekera-Dolgopolov process. Moreover, we demonstrate that mtmsl\eb on any domain evolves in time according to the Karlin-McGregor process, thereby explaining the branching mechanisms underlying various loop ensembles. This includes the multi-time Karlin-McGregor process's specific parameters which determine the statistics of branching points and branching numbers. We also discover that mtmsl\eb on any domain generates a looptree whose statistics match those of a continuous random tree whose edges are labeled with the areas of the branches. We establish this labeling process as a continuous random tree labeled by surface order, a new and distinct invariant of the mtmsl\eb process. into a sophisticated collaborative platform for developing high-quality manuscripts
and software projects. Originally developed at McMaster University's theoretical
biology lab, WorkingWiki enables multiple users to work together on a range of
tasks by utilizing command-line tools to translate raw'source code' into desired outputs.
Its features cater specifically to programmers and researchers who use languages
like R, Python, and C, and it boasts specialized tools for seamless LaTeX editing.
By integrating features from collaborative editors, development environments,
version control systems, and publishing platforms, WorkingWiki unlocks the
full potential of wiki-based collaboration, and its customizable'makefiles'
and modular architecture enable users to tailor and repurpose its functionality. The extension's numerous innovations also tackle longstanding challenges
in software development, such as automating testing, managing dependencies,
and securing collaboration through simple, encrypted data exchanges. Despite its
advanced capabilities, WorkingWiki is remarkably easy to use, and its guidance
is woven into the wiki itself, making it an ideal tool for teaching best practices in software development and research. The extension's unique features and

This study undertakes a linear analysis of a methane-air jet flame experiencing turbulence to determine its response to acoustic vibrations emitted from upstream, while factoring in temperature fluctuations that can cause instability in flames. To accurately predict flame behavior in a linearized model, it is crucial to account for heat released from the flame's fluctuations. Unlike previous studies, the current work utilizes an active flame approach that considers how heat released from the flame's fluctuations respond to acoustic vibrations. To apply this approach in a linear framework, combustion models must be linearized, which is shown to be challenging using existing models such as LES and DNS. Nevertheless, RANS models prove to be effective alternatives due to their ability to avoid closure issues. To apply these models, the researchers used LES to obtain the average flow conditions of the jet flame. An analysis of the results showed that a linearized RANS-Eddy Break-Up model yields the most accurate representation of reaction rates compared to other models, while an analysis of the model's equations revealed that reaction rate oscillations result from the disruption of Kelvin-Helmholtz vortex rings within the jet flame. Furthermore, the results from the model matched the outcomes from the LES simulations, confirming its effectiveness. Finally, the application of this model led to the identification of a reaction rate reservoir within the jet flame that resists linear response to acoustic vibrations, causing a delay in reaction rates that contributes to the instability of the jet flame. This phenomenon was demonstrated to be unaffected by the direction of acoustic vibrations applied. Consequently, this study demonstrates that the disintegration of Kelvin-Helmholtz vortex rings within jet flames leads to reaction rate oscillations, which in turn contributes to instability in the presence of acoustic vibrations. This knowledge can be utilized to improve the performance of flame stabilization techniques in the presence of turbulence and turbulence-induced instability. Nonlocal gravity theory is a classical generalization of Einstein's gravity theory. Based on an analogy with nonlocal electrodynamics, this new model involves a history-dependent relation that can be confirmed through data. The purpose of this paper is to modify nonlocal gravity theory so that the nonlocal aspect relates directly to observable properties, similar to the approach in nonlocal electrodynamics. The reformulated theory results in a constitutive relation identical to one proposed recently by Puetzfeld, Obukhov, and Hehl. The nonlocal gravity theory can be applied to show that de Sitter spacetime does not meet the theory's requirements. The paper also examines the nonlocal version of the Einstein-Hilbert differential action and determines its critical value. The impact of the nonlocal effect on the Einstein gravity equation is investigated mathematically, and the paper concludes with a discussion of the relation between nonlocal gravity and dark energy. The approach used in this paper can be applied to nonlocal modifications of other metric theories of gravity. The result that de Sitter spacetime does not satisfy the theory's requirements implies that the nonlocal gravity theory cannot support the Big Bang theory, however, this result can be interpreted differently in different contexts. The paper also presents some mathematical expressions that were previously confirmed numerically. The discussion on the relation between nonlocal gravity and dark energy provides the paper with additional relevance to the 2011 Max-Planck research award that was focused on understanding the connection between nonlocal gravity and the observed dark energy effect in the universe. The paper's mathematical content can be applied to models of the universe such as the Friedmann-Lema\itre model. Observations of some variable X-ray sources within the Milky Way's center that have shown no outbursts in over a decade have led some researchers to suggest a significant population of stellar mass black holes in the region. A crucial aspect of the theory that these sources are actually black holes is the claim that neutron star binaries with low masses exhibit recurring X-ray bursts within short intervals. This study contradicts that idea by revealing that about half of the known LMXBs, featuring a neutron star as the primary component, exhibit outburst recurrence times exceeding a decade when detected by the MAXI telescope. Moreover, to reconcile the total population of neutron star binaries with observed and radio pulsar populations within the Milky Way, researchers find that a significant majority of these binaries have recurrence times exceeding a century for outbursts visible to the MAXI telescope and most remain undiscovered. The observed pattern of recurrence times also diverges from a linear relationship, instead showing a significant slowdown as time goes by. This observation can be attributed to a power law relationship with an index of approximately 1.5, likely the result of a distribution of binary angles rather than a constant spin loss acceleration. This study's findings also highlight the possibility of identifying LMXBs with short recurrence times, particularly those featuring a millisecond pulsar as the primary component, using a combination of radio pulsar surveys and wide-field X-ray observations over the next few decades. The estimated number of such binaries with recurrence times exceeding a decade for X-ray outbursts is approximately 240 within the Milky Way. The research suggests that the majority of these binaries are likely powered by accretion from the interstellar medium rather than a companion star and could be distinguished by searching for repeated X-ray outbursts from the same location over a period of twenty to thirty years. The study estimates that about 40 of these isolated neutron star binaries with short recurrence times could be found within the Milky Way. The observed relationship between neutron stars in low mass X-ray binaries and their transient recurrence times can be explained by considering the dynamics of both the binaries themselves and the search space, rather than their physical properties. The study provides a comprehensive model that incorporates both factors and offers a promising lead in discovering a significant population of neutron stars with recurrence times for outbursts visible to the MAXI telescope. Improving neural conversational agents' ability to produce diverse, engaging responses in casual conversations is a challenge. To tackle this issue, this paper introduces two significant innovations. Firstly, it proposes a new assessment metric that employs Natural Language Inference to gauge the semantic variety of responses generated by the model in a conversation. Using a previously established framework, this metric was tested and showed a clear connection between Natural Language Inference Diversity and semantic variety. It was discovered that the contradiction relation yields more precise results than the neutral relation in measuring diversity and integrating the NLI model's confidence achieves the highest performance to date. Secondly, this paper demonstrates a way to enhance the semantic variety of responses generated by the model through an iterative procedure called Diversity Threshold Generation, which, in comparison to standard generation methods, results in an average 137% improvement in NLI Diversity. This technique's effectiveness is proven across five different conversational datasets, including the recently introduced Spoken Dialog Diversity Dataset. The implementation, datasets, and evaluations are all part of the code package that is accessible online. When applied to a generative model using the iterative approach, the code package also includes models that exhibit diverse response characteristics for evaluation purposes. This research is an initial step towards evaluating the semantic variety of responses generated by the model and provides a foundation for future work aimed at improving the diversity of responses in conversational interactions. This paper is based on the work presented at the Conference on Empirical Methods in Natural Language Processing (EMNLP) in 2023. The current version contains revisions made based on feedback from reviewers. The original version was published as a paper at EMNLP 2023 and an earlier version of the research was published as a paper at the Annual Conference of the North American Chapter of the Association for Computational Linguistics (NAACL) in 2022. The research mentioned in this paper also received support from the following projects: the Key-Area Research and Development Program of Guangdong, the Science and Technology Planning Project of Guangzhou, and the Research Fund for the Doctoral Program of Higher Education of China. Computer simulations model rotating low-mass stars with the capability for sustained nuclear reactions, considering a range of rotation rates, rather than slow rotation alone. Using these simulations, we determined the boundaries within which stars could maintain nuclear energy through hydrogen burning. These boundaries varied based on angular momentum. However, above a certain threshold (approximately 8.85 x 10^48 erg s) the boundaries broke into two distinct branches, resulting from objects losing mass and experiencing extreme spin. This research was applied to model the development of sub-stellar objects. Two possible scenarios were modeled: one with external forces gradually slowing the star, mainly controlled by spin-down time, and another where the star spins out of control, ultimately shedding mass and shrinking. Specifically, for the self-destructing stars, the conditions for hydrogen burning were met for masses between 0.01 and 0.44 solar masses. Becker-Denef-Lipschitz first observed in 1979 that over finite fields $k$, the total residue map $\text{res}$ from Laurent series to $k$ is expressible in a specific language, provided $t$ is included as a parameter. This discovery motivated further research into the properties of a specific mathematical theory related to valued fields. In the course of these investigations, the authors proved that this theory does not have a certain desirable feature and demonstrated that, for infinite fields $k$, the associated power series fields cannot be computationally decided. This, in turn, led to an analogous undecidability conclusion for a specific complex-valued field of power series. In addition, the authors established that the ring of integers from the $p$-adic field $\mathbb{Q}_p$ cannot be effectively determined when $p$ is greater than two, as it is equivalent to the undecidability of the $p$-adic field itself. In a related context, the authors also examined the relationship between the geometry of trees to fields with a specific property, known as "minimal" width, and in the process, they discovered an error in an earlier publication by MacKay. Furthermore, they extended and refined an earlier result by Goodstein, which in turn built upon an earlier finding by Schanuel. A natural extension of the Becker-Denef-Lipschitz question, initially proposed in 1979, is also addressed. This extension involves fields with a non-Archimedean absolute value, specifically the field with $p$-adic numbers from a finite extension of $\mathbb{Q}_p$, denoted as $\mathbb{Z}_p(\sqrt{d})$, where $d$ is a nonzero integer valued in $\mathbb{Z}_p$ and has a specific property known as "weak divisibility". A novel analysis into the causes of performance degradation through cache eviction was also performed, leading to the discovery of an unknown source of slowdowns.  Compared to existing techniques, HyperDegrade resulted in more significant slowdowns and improvements, which in certain cases achieved an enhanced time granularity of three orders of magnitude for Flush+Reload attacks.  To further evaluate the technique, metrics for side-channel leakage were proposed, which demonstrated that HyperDegrade could be effective in side-channel amplification without compromising data integrity. A localized alteration in knot diagrams is referred to as an unknotting operation. It can be demonstrated that any knot diagram can be converted into a trivial unknot through a sequence of unknotting operations, combined with some variations in the diagram configuration, which are referred to as Reidemeister moves. Unknotting operations hold significant value in the field of knot theory; they serve a purpose in analyzing the intricacy of knots and knot-related properties. Moreover, they also have implications in the fields of biology, chemistry, and physics for studying complexly intertwined structures of molecules, substances, and DNA. The purpose of this paper was to introduce a novel type of unknotting operation, which is called the diagonal move, applicable to classical and welded knots. The study shows that the cross-over change, the delta-move, the sharp-move, the gamma-move, the n-gon move, the pass move, and the 4-move can be achieved by applying a sequence of diagonal moves. The study also delves into defining a distance measure that originates from the diagonal move, as well as examining its characteristics. The study on the distance measure reveals that it satisfies the criteria of being a metric, which is referred to as the diagonal distance. The study also compares the metric properties of the diagonal distance with those of the classical distance measures already identified in the literature, which include the number of crossings, the number of twists, the 4-move distance, the n-gon distance, the pass distance, the sharp distance, the gamma distance, the delta distance, the welded distance, the volume distance, the energy distance, the protein distance, and the chemical distance. The study reveals that the distance measures already identified in the literature can be achieved by applying a sequence of the diagonal move, which is referred to as the relationship of the 1-Delta rule. The study also defines the term chemical distance, which is a measure that originates from the reaction rule called the delta-move, as well as examining its properties. The study on the chemical distance reveals that it satisfies the criteria of being a metric, which is referred to as the chemical distance measure. The study also compares the metric properties of the chemical distance measure with those of the classical distance measures already identified in the literature. This discovery builds on a preceding finding by the second listed author, proving that I(X) integrated over the Gramain 1-cycles generates the Casson invariant, a singular, nontrivial Vassiliev invariant of order two after accounting for scalar multiplication factors. Similarities can be drawn with a part of Mortier's research. Nonetheless, in contrast to but also inspired by his result, we derive our cocycle, I(X), through the use of graph-based configuration space integrals rather than combinatorial approaches used by Mortier. In this context, we explore a privacy-preserving approach called federated learning that enables several entities to train a robust machine learning model jointly, without exchanging sensitive information about their data. Based on how entities cooperate, FL can be categorized into two primary forms - horizontal and vertical FL. The former involves participants who collaborate using identical data attributes, while in the latter, entities with overlapping sample IDs collaborate using different features. Given its versatility, vertical FL is deemed particularly suitable for collaborative training by major enterprises. Here we concentrate on FL and delve into possible privacy breaches in actual VFL implementations. Two applicable attacks were created by us - one is called a reverse multiplication attack designed to circumvent logistic regression, while the other, known as a reverse sum attack, targets XGBoost protocols. Our empirical study validates that both attacks are successful, effective, evasive, and straightforward - they do not diverge from the predefined protocol, nor do they lower the model's accuracy; even with data encrypted. Additionally, we found out the stolen information can train a new machine learning classifier which is just as accurate as the one trained using actual data, without knowing beforehand much about the target user. Our analysis highlights potential preventive strategies, while revealing challenges that might give rise to several exciting research opportunities. Kernel methods have proven highly effective in various machine learning applications, yet their scalability to large datasets is severely limited due to the computationally expensive nature of pairwise evaluations. In response, Random Fourier Features were proposed to approximate kernel functions using randomized transformations, thereby enabling the use of kernel methods on larger data sets. While widely adopted, this method has significant drawbacks, notably requiring an unnecessarily large number of features, directly proportional to the size of the dataset, in order to achieve satisfactory results comparable to traditional kernel-based methods. In order to circumvent these limitations and efficiently process large datasets, this paper introduces an alternative method of kernel approximation that leverages insights specific to the underlying data and offers both feature dimensionality reduction and performance enhancements. We test and evaluate this novel method against a range of competitors, including RFF, orthogonal random features, and the Nyström method. Notably, our method is found to consistently outperform RFF, often to a significant degree, and also compares favourably to orthogonal random features and the Nyström method in various scenarios. In addition to its scalable kernel approximation capabilities, this method can be configured to efficiently utilize meta-information, thereby enabling the construction of compact and informative kernel representations from sampled data. In our study, we demonstrated how both a group that operates on a set in a recurring manner and a diagonal group are effectively incorporated into the wreath products under their combined, or product action, utilizing the Cartesian Decomposition technique. By applying this method, we established a significant connection between the group that acts on the set and its diagonal group, thereby establishing a connection between them through the wreath products. This connection enables us to conclude that the set's invariant properties under the combined action are identical to the properties of the set in relation to the diagonal group's action, which can be determined using the Fourier-Wielandt norm. This achievement leads to an enhancement of previous results by Kowalski and Troi, where we have now removed the requirement for the set's initial property to be extremely large. Additionally, our findings complement the results obtained by Diaconis and O'Connell. In the case where the set's invariant properties are expressed as polynomial equations and the diagonal group's properties meet a specific standard, which we defined, we demonstrated how the Fourier-Wielandt norm can be utilized to determine the polynomial's roots. This, in turn, enables us to conclude that the set's properties will converge quickly to the properties of the diagonal group, even after a large number of random permutations have been applied. This result is particularly notable since it extends the earlier findings obtained by Heyde and Szpankowski in a related context. Our research also includes an evaluation of the Fourier-Wielandt norm's value, which can be viewed as a measure of the distance between the set's properties and the properties of the diagonal group, as well as an examination of its relationship with other norms, which were previously defined. Furthermore, we explored certain regularity properties of the Fourier-Wielandt norm, which can be utilized to assess the set's properties in relation to the standard we defined, as well as its connection to the entropy measure, which was previously established by Diaconis and Shahshahani. Our study provides a framework for understanding the regularity of the Fourier-Wielandt norm, which is a regular measure that can be characterized through its relationship with the Cartesian Decomposition technique and the entropy measure, which is a measure of the set's properties that operates on the set in a recurring manner. This framework enables us to conclude that the Fourier-Wielandt norm's regularity standard is equivalent to the standard defined by the entropy measure, as well as the set's properties that operate on the set in a recurring manner

This research paper examines conformally flat hypersurfaces of n-dimensional space (n is 4 or higher) within a hypersphere of n+2 dimensions. We start by classifying and describing these conformally flat hypersurfaces when they have constant M\"obius curvature under specific transformations. Next, we prove that a compact hypersurface with this constant M\"obius curvature, denoted R, is specifically equal to $(n-1)(n-2)r^2$ for values of r less than 1. Furthermore, if this hypersurface is compact, we establish that it is topologically equivalent to a torus defined by the union of a circle with a radius of $\sqrt{1-r^2}$ and a hypersphere with a radius of r in the space of n+1 dimensions. If this hypersurface is not compact, we found that it can be represented as a union of a line in the space of n+1 dimensions and a hypersphere with a radius of r in the space of n+2 dimensions. If this hypersurface has constant scalar curvature under the M\"obius transformation, we also investigated and generalized its equations to provide a deeper understanding of these conformally flat hypersurfaces. This research was inspired by a 1973 paper by Calabi, a 1982 paper by Chen and Gonoza, and a 1991 paper by Esposito, Maximo, and Riera. It also builds upon a problem proposed by Daniel Gelfand in 1993. It is worth noting that the terms "scalar curvature" and "M\"obius curvature" are used interchangeably in this research. Network vulnerability assessment is crucial for creating strategies to prevent the spread of malicious information and diseases in networks. Researchers often study network immunization, but traditional approaches typically focus on broad measures, such as network criticality and component size. In contrast, this paper delves into a micro-level analysis, where the removal of individual nodes during an attack is examined in detail. Based on percolation theory, the authors analyze the effects of removing a single node that causes other nodes to disconnect from the main component. Specifically, this paper investigates the number of nodes that become disconnected from the main component as a result of removing one node. By applying this micro-level approach to a random attack on a Cayley tree network, the distribution of the resulting node removal sizes is derived. Furthermore, threshold values are established to determine when the removal of an individual node leads to the main component breaking into two or more distinct components. Additionally, the average size of the removed component is calculated and analyzed to reveal key properties. Interestingly, it is found that when the average removed component size exceeds 1, it indicates that the network is fragmented as a result of the random attack. This paper also explores applications to network spin glass models and provides a theoretical framework for understanding the effects of targetted node removal during an attack. Finally, the paper discusses potential extensions to its methods and presents numerical results for various network sizes. Experimental data from Wikipedia citation networks and a rock music collaboration network are used for model validation. The detection capabilities of advanced gravitational wave detectors are hindered in the high-frequency range by the quantum limitations of measurement and signal loss in optical recycling systems. Overcoming this constraint is critical for identifying gravitational waves generated by binary neutron star mergers. We present the concept of the sloshing Sagnac interferometer topology, an innovative variation of the Michelson design where the end mirrors are optically linked to form an additional resonating cavity. By transforming the detector into a system with multiple coupled cavities, this design outperforms the conventional signal-recycled Michelson setup by overcoming optical loss-induced limitations. Using advanced parameters similar to LIGO+, this new design offers improved sensitivity at high frequencies or better signal-to-noise ratios for specific binary neutron star merger waveforms, offering promising possibilities for future gravitational wave detectors. This research focuses on creating resilient Molmer-Sorensen gates using trapped ions arranged in a line, incorporating Gaussian amplitude modulation and a consistent laser frequency. We chose a frequency that maintains balanced entanglement accumulation across all motion modes to provide a significant degree of protection against frequency errors, particularly for long chains of ions. A demonstration of this method is performed on a chain of three ions, achieving an average reduction of under one percent from peak precision within a twenty kilohertz range of frequency deviation, and the efficiency of this gate design is examined through numerical simulations on chains consisting of two to thirty-three ions. We found that this gate design yields minimal loss of frequency robustness as the number of ions increases, making it suitable for large-scale quantum machines. Additionally, this design exhibits an entropy growth rate that is roughly half of the total entropy generation for both two- and thirty-three-ion chains, demonstrating its versatile applications. This research is an initial step towards developing more intricate quantum gates that can withstand frequency errors, and potential areas of investigation are also considered. We have made the necessary Python codes available at https://github.com/Jiawei-Li-2021/Robust_MSM_Gate. By analyzing the process of $K^+ \to \pi^0 e^+ N$, they determined the present limit can be set at $2\times 10^{-6}$ for a particular lepton interaction with masses ranging from 125 to 144 MeV, a region that current production searches lack in depth. Combining existing data with optimized detection tools or improved photon rejection techniques can significantly narrow this limit. Neural language models have largely surpassed $N$-gram models due to better performance, but our findings suggest that $n$-gram models still excel in many situations with low computational costs, demonstrating a strong foundation of language understanding. Building upon this discovery, we developed a neural model that learns from the remaining knowledge between $n$-gram models and the true language distribution, allowing for both a deeper grasp of language and the flexibility to adjust models through the $n$-gram base without altering the neural model. Through extensive experiments on tasks including language modeling, machine translation, and summarization, our hybrid approach consistently delivers enhanced performance over standard neural models and facilitates seamless domain adaptation by simply swapping the $n$-gram base, eliminating the need for additional training. Reconstructing three-dimensional faces in complex real-world scenarios poses significant difficulties due to frequently missing or occluded facial details, particularly in images depicting large head orientations. This challenging problem is compounded by the extensive variability of head poses, which significantly expands the potential solution space and complicates modeling efforts. To break down this complex task into more manageable components, our approach focuses on modeling both pose and occlusion. In this regard, we introduce an end-to-end framework called SADRNet, which produces a face that varies based on the orientation and another face that remains invariant, then fuses these faces via a self-alignment mechanism informed by occlusion. Exhaustive testing of our proposed technique on the widely used AFLW2000-3D and Florence datasets shows substantial performance enhancements over existing top-ranking methods. Moreover, our approach achieves competitive results with respect to current state-of-the-art methods on the large-scale datasets AFLW3000-3D and REFA. Our code is available at https://github.com/zwang84/SADRNet.

In an effort to enhance the efficacy of this system in capturing data from vote tabulation, we propose an innovative approach that incorporates the use of logical rules in conjunction with the existing spell-checking capability. Our experimental evaluation of this integrated system showed a substantial improvement in data capture accuracy, with results indicating that it can correctly capture data from vote tabulation documents with a high degree of accuracy even in the presence of common spelling errors. In contrast, the performance of the conventional iOCR system significantly lags behind this integrated system, albeit it still performs better than traditional OCR systems. In such cases, the integrated system demonstrates a significantly higher performance than the conventional iOCR system. In recent years, significant progress made by large-scale models has underscored the relevance of statistical models featuring multiple parameters. Research has been conducted to evaluate linear models with numerous parameters in high-dimensional environments characterized by non-sparse data. These studies typically assume the independence of data samples, but the current research extends beyond this limitation by exploring a linear regression model with time series data under conditions of over-parameterization, where data samples are inherently interdependent. A key factor for maintaining stability in future low-carbon power grids is expected to be energy storage systems. Studies examining past experiences reveal a common issue with storage units - they frequently fail to take advantage of high-price signals during periods of low energy supply. This behavior has been often attributed to inaccurate forecasting or operational issues. However, our research suggests a more plausible explanation is rooted in risk-averse decision-making practices. Utilizing a stochastic self-scheduling approach and real data from the Australian electricity market, our findings show that risk-conscious storage units prioritize short-term cost savings by engaging in local price speculation, and tend to ignore opportunities in periods with unusual price fluctuations. This has significant policy implications, given the difficulty of detecting and managing storage units' risk aversion. Given the inherent challenges in altering a unit's risk tolerance, our recommendation is to focus on developing risk-affordable scheduling mechanisms that accommodate the inherent risk-averse nature of storage units. This approach has the potential to channel more of the grid's storage capacity towards optimizing economic and risk-based outcomes. 

A stochastic self-scheduling model has been proposed for risk-conscious energy storage units. This model leverages a convex tractable approximation to ensure optimal solutions are computationally efficient to obtain. A major advantage of this approach is that it allows for easy integration into existing day-ahead markets with minimal modification. Furthermore, our approach enables storage units to manage multiple risk management strategies, including full risk-neutral scheduling as a special case. The validity and effectiveness of this approach have been validated through comparative studies involving real-world data and simulations covering various market conditions. This includes evaluation of optimal scheduling payoffs, risk profiles, and operational costs in relation to benchmark approaches. The results show that compared to other risk management strategies, the proposed approach yields the most desirable outcomes in terms of a trade-off between economic benefits and risk aversion. Our investigation focused on the transport properties of HgTe quantum wells near their critical thickness, where the energy gap is minimal, and the energy spectrum is described by a singular Dirac cone structure. Both large and small-sized (mesoscopic) samples were examined as part of this study. When looking at small-sized samples, a well-defined, quantized resistance emerged at low magnetic field strength due to Landau filling, and was closely related to helical edge states that form around the neutral point of the samples. Conversely, larger samples showed significant resistance oscillations in low-magnetic-field conditions. This behavior is attributed to interaction between the neutral state at the edge and a non-neutral hole Landau level within the bulk material. A hypothetical model incorporating a reservoir formed by heavy holes has been developed as an explanatory framework. Moreover, both the magnitude of the resistance and the number of oscillations demonstrated a strong correlation with the magnitude of the magnetic field applied, and a specific resistance value was obtained for zero-magnetic-field conditions. This result is particularly notable given the challenge of measuring resistance in samples with a minimal energy gap while being subjected to a magnetic field. Our study highlights the unique properties of HgTe quantum wells and the prominent role that the neutral state plays in their transport characteristics. This discovery also presents an intriguing application, with the ability to control a sensitive, magnetoresistive element using a magnetic field, causing the resistance to fluctuate between two distinct states. This phenomenon is stable and can be maintained for an extended period of time. This research demonstrates a prominent advantage of using HgTe quantum wells, with the ability to function as sensitive magnetoresistive elements in devices, potentially leading to innovative applications in physics research. Our research team suggests that the unique properties of these elements could also be adapted for use in spintronics and other advanced technologies, where the presence of a neutral state at the edge of samples offers great potential for optimizing magnetic field sensing capabilities. This optimization is achieved by adjusting the thickness of the samples to match the size of the neutral state, ensuring that the majority of the current flows through the neutral edge channel rather than the bulk material. As a result, we observed a significant enhancement of the magnetic field sensitivity in our experiments, with a maximum value of approximately 37 $\mu$V/T detected. In Dynamic Time-Division Duplexing (TDD), individual cells can schedule uplink and downlink modes independently, depending on local traffic conditions, but this causes interference between neighboring cells, turning a critical problem into an NP-hard mixed-integer non-convex challenge. We've developed an efficient and localized solution, separating power allocation and scheduling processes, first assigning power independently to cells, followed by a non-cooperative game determining scheduling modes, with payoffs calculated according to the level of interference and required cell communication. Simulations, set in an outdoor scenario with multiple small cells, reveal our method outperforms static TDD solutions. Moreover, our approach can be easily expanded to account for various TDD scheduling modes and various types of cellular infrastructure. Ultimately, this research demonstrates the effectiveness of dynamic TDD scheduling in challenging, high-density cellular environments.

In this work, we introduce a novel meta-learning framework centered on ODE neural networks, which acquires an understanding of gradients. This framework grants optimizers enhanced flexibility and infuses an automatic inductive bias into tasks, as we have found. Through the simplest Hamiltonian Neural Network implementation, our method proves more effective than a comparable LSTM-based meta-learner for a simulated task and MNIST with ReLU activations in the model being optimized, as well as consistently outperforming traditional optimization techniques for the artificial task and delivering results on par with standard optimization for MNIST. Additionally, our approach demonstrates the ability to efficiently optimize natural language processing models for the SuperGLUE benchmark, achieving comparable performance at a significant reduction in cost (20-30 times) when compared to traditional optimization methods. This is attributed to the improved generalization capability of our optimizer following the training process, as supported by post-hoc evaluation using the annealing method, which helps to identify an optimal temperature that corresponds to our implementation's ease of parameter updating. We believe that our simple, efficient, and versatile model of an optimizer, which we have made publicly available, will be beneficial to the community by enabling the exploration of new applications and methodologies for meta-learning. In particular, we propose using the learned dynamics of an optimizer as a basis to develop more sophisticated models, which we term 'dynamic meta-learning'. This approach has the advantage of eliminating the need to repeat the meta-learning process when modifying existing tasks, as the optimizer's learned dynamics automatically adapt to these changes, as we have observed in the experiments conducted. We have made our code and models available at https://github.com/tinghui/hamiltonein. We hope this contributes to the ongoing discussion on the benefits and limitations of static and dynamic models of optimizers within the meta-learning community. Furthermore, we have an interactive web-based dashboard to visualize the dynamics of our learned optimizer for the NLP tasks at https://tinghui.org/optimizer. We have an associated paper talking about the general concept, methodology and findings of this work, which can be found here: https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.01308. Simply enhancing a machine learning model's accuracy is not sufficient, as we must also focus on increasing its reliability. This consideration is crucial for creating robust AI systems that are capable of withstanding critical situations in areas like transportation, finance, and medical fields. We recommend developing a collaborative multi-agent framework that combines artificial intelligence with human input. This proposed system involves two key components: a scoring agent that calculates a reliability metric for each prediction, penalizing both overoptimistic and overly cautious results; and a refinement agent that utilizes a set of human-defined safety guidelines to identify and rectify unusual instances. It then uses these corrected examples to update its model through transfer learning. We put the proposed system through testing on datasets modified to contain artificial errors and found that it effectively improves both the accuracy and reliability of the model with only a limited increase in training data. Furthermore, our proposed method demonstrates comparable performance to other robust learning techniques in machine learning, such as adversarial training and regularization methods, but requires significantly smaller sample sizes. Consequently, this framework presents a promising solution for enhancing the trustworthiness of machine learning models in high-stakes settings. We also offer potential directions for future development, such as incorporating the framework into cutting-edge machine learning models and conducting scalability tests on larger datasets. Prior research on machine learning reliability focused on methods like adversarial training and regularization, which attempt to enhance a model's robustness by manipulating its structure or input data, but often require substantial additional data for training. In contrast, our proposed approach takes advantage of existing datasets, making it appealing for applications with limited data. Ultimately, we believe that model reliability should be an integral part of machine learning design, rather than an afterthought. We have made the code for our proposed framework available on GitHub, which can be accessed through the following link: https://github.com/Zhiyu Jordan/ Reliable-Machine-Learning. We have also included an illustrative example of how to incorporate the framework into transfer learning, in addition to providing code for the robust machine learning framework. We propose a collaborative multi-agent framework that combines artificial intelligence with human input to enhance the trustworthiness of machine learning models. We demonstrate the effectiveness of this framework by conducting experiments on datasets modified to contain artificial errors and show that it efficiently improves both the accuracy and reliability of the model using a limited amount of additional data. We also explore potential directions for future development, such as incorporating the framework into cutting-edge machine learning models and conducting scalability tests on larger datasets. A newly defined polynomial, referred to as the nth toroidal colored Jones polynomial, is established for links in a thickened torus. Dubbed $J_n^T$, this polynomial demonstrates numerous properties similar to the original colored Jones polynomial, and notably displays volume conjecture behavior. By applying $J_n^T$, we prove the volume conjecture holds true for a specific link, and provide computational data suggesting it holds for additional links. Moreover, $J_n^T$ can be represented through two distinct constructions, a pseudo-operator invariant, and a construction rooted in the Kauffman bracket skein module of the torus. Notably, $J_n^T$ yields invariants for virtual and biperiodic links, providing an instance of volume conjecture behavior in a virtual link. In the process, we establish that the standard volume construction satisfies the volume conjecture. The resulting $J_n^T$ polynomial can be calculated for links with a certain property, referred to as being volume-dependent-on-the-frame. The associated heuristic framework can be applied to various links, including those identified by means of a specific type of closure called the standard closure. The volume conjecture, initially proposed by Witten, is comprised of three distinct conjectures related to polynomials associated with links in a 3-dimensional space with a specific property. The development mentioned above constitutes a breakthrough in understanding the volume conjecture, particularly with regards to its second part, and provides a comprehensive examination of the associated framework. The resulting polynomial, $J_n^T$, can be applied to calculate the volume of links in a 3-dimensional space with a specific property, specifically those identified by means of a closure called the standard closure, offering a novel framework for the second part of the volume conjecture. The primary objective of Word Sense Disambiguation (WSD) involves determining the appropriate sense of a word with multiple meanings within a particular context.  Advances in deep learning, specifically utilizing BERT, have led to significant progress in this area, with several strategies being developed to combine structured knowledge for enhanced performance.  Additionally, multiple data augmentation techniques have been discovered to be valuable tools in natural language processing tasks.  Building on prior work incorporating BERT and WordNet knowledge, this study explores various data augmentation techniques in context-gloss pairs to enhance the efficacy of WSD.  Experimental results indicate that both sentence and word-level augmentation strategies are effective in addressing WSD, while the incorporation of hypernyms' definitions from a lexical knowledge base can further improve performance.  A comparative analysis of different context-gloss augmentation techniques is conducted, revealing that the application of back translation to definitions produces the most satisfactory outcomes.  Furthermore, the study validates the reliability of developed models, as well as the ease with which they can be applied to other natural language processing tasks involving semantic analysis. The CMS experiment at the CERN LHC detected the production of top quarks for the first time using proton-lead data at an 8.16 TeV nucleon-nucleon center-of-mass energy. Top quark production was identified in events featuring one isolated electron or muon and four or more jets, from a data set totaling 174 inverse nanobarns of luminosity. The measured signal exceeded the five-standard-deviation threshold expected for a background-only hypothesis, and the cross-sectional measurement for top quark pairs was found to be 45 nanobarns with an 8-nanobarn uncertainty, consistent with theoretical predictions from quantum chromodynamics. Additionally, the measurement was used to estimate the total quark-gluon plasma jet density in proton-lead collisions at this energy level, and constraints were placed on certain modified parton distribution functions. The findings also demonstrated that the phase space available for top quark physics in the LHC with proton beams is limited, and experiments with larger center-of-mass energies, such as the future 13-14 TeV LHC with lead-lead collisions, are necessary for more comprehensive studies of top quark production and quark-gluon plasma properties. The research was based on data from the 2016 run of the CMS experiment and involved significant improvements to the top quark identification techniques and event selection processes. The results were submitted for consideration at the 2022 Meeting of the Division of Particles and Fields of the American Physical Society. This study focuses on key elements in cross-domain text-to-SQL parsing, specifically schema linking and value filling. To enhance encoding abilities, a column selection auxiliary task is proposed, leveraging explicit targets for relevance matching. Additionally, two value filling approaches are presented to bridge the gap between current zero-shot parsers and practical applications, considering that many existing parsers overlook value filling in synthesized SQL. Experiments on the Spider dataset demonstrate the superiority of our proposed framework over baseline models in terms of execution and exact set match accuracy when database contents are inaccessible, with further analysis pointing to areas for future improvement. Nonetheless, due to the fragmented nature of value filling in Spider, a larger scale dataset is necessary for a more comprehensive evaluation. Nonetheless, our proposed scheme has the potential to be extended to other SQL datasets with embedded value information, providing a viable foundation for future research. Our code and models are available at https://github.com/zhong-jian/hred-zsps.

This paper delves into the utilization of differential privacy within the framework of graph-based data. It outlines the DP formulations relevant to publishing graphs, statistical analysis associated with graphs, and machine learning on graph-based data, including graph neural networks. However, applying DP to graph data poses significant challenges due to interconnected data points that can form complex relationships. This issue is compounded by a lack of universally accepted DP formulation in graph-based contexts. This problem further exacerbates the difficulty in conducting private machine learning on graph data. A notable absence of systematised research on graph-based learning in relation to privacy was a key driver of our work, leading us to explore various formulations of DP on graphs, discuss associated challenges and promising applications including GNNs. This work also compares and distinguishes different graph-based learning tasks from those that incorporate graph neural networks. Ultimately, our work is concluded by examining open research questions and exploring possible avenues for further investigation in this domain. This work is pertinent to a broad range of topics including deep learning on graphs, graph-based recommendation systems, and learning on molecular graphs particularly in the context of drug discovery. Researchers have successfully used hydrodynamic theories to simulate complex dynamics of quantum many-body systems, and in this work, we've developed a novel stochastic hydrodynamic approach for describing interacting Bose gases within a specific phase-space framework. This method extends previous hydrodynamic methods, enabling the simulation of a system's full quantum dynamics and allowing for the calculation of non-equilibrium correlations, even for short-wavelength phenomena. The annealed large deviation principle (LDP) for the empirical process of words is characterized by a rate function that equals the specific relative entropy of the observed distribution of words with respect to the reference distribution of words.  For renewal times with an algebraic tail, a quenched LDP (conditioned on a typical sequence of letters) was established by Birkner, Greven, and den Hollander, which resulted in a rate function consisting of two components, including the annealed rate function and another component proportional to the specific relative entropy of the observed distribution of letters relative to the reference distribution of letters, obtained by combining the words and randomizing the starting point.  The proportionality constant was found to be equal to the tail exponent of the renewal process.  The purpose of this study is to extend both LDPs to sequences of letters that are not independent and identically distributed by demonstrating that both principles can be applied to sequences of letters satisfying a condition known as summable variation, which provides the necessary condition for both principles to be applicable, while neither of the reference laws involved in the rate functions is independent and identically distributed. We define a new concept of relative 1-homotopy type for mappings between a surface and a metric space that contains a specified set of Jordan curves, and investigate its properties. This enables us to prove the existence and local smoothness of the surfaces with minimal area within a particular relative 1-homotopy class in certain types of metric spaces. Furthermore, we establish that when the ambient space has a certain topological characteristic, maps that are relatively 1-homotopic are also relatively homotopic. These findings also hold for closed surfaces and improve previous results of several mathematicians. The approach used in our work utilizes a novel form of a relative Rayleigh quotient and results from the theory of the classical Rayleigh quotient. In addition, we contribute to the study of surfaces with minimal area within a given relative 1-homotopy class by obtaining new information about their analytic properties, specifically with regards to the local smoothness of their points of minimal area. This extends the findings of several renowned mathematicians, including Guo,  Meng,  and  Esposito,  and  provides a more detailed understanding of the behavior of surfaces with minimal area in domains that contain sharp corners. In such cases, we demonstrate that the surfaces with minimal area are composed of straight rays and circular arcs, and we define their local regularity through the use of a new concept that takes into consideration their geometric configuration. Moreover, we identify the conditions under which the points of minimal area exhibit local H\"older regularity. In addition, we contribute to the study of closed surfaces with minimal area by determining their possible shapes and classifying them into distinct categories, and we demonstrate that the surfaces with minimal area are consistently smooth outside the polar regions, except in the case of the cone, which was previously known, as well as the sphere, which was also previously known, and a new category that we term the pillow. Moreover, our study reveals that the optimal parameters obtained are excessively sensitive to the manner in which the data is divided, often resulting in suboptimal solutions and significant difficulties in achieving reproducibility. Experimental findings confirm our proposed approach yields superior results than conventional methods, as measured by model performance and parameter robustness. We investigated the absorption of a single, monochromatic light beam at 689 nm as it passes through a cloud of ultracold $^{88}$Sr atoms. Due to the interaction, the absorption pattern deviates significantly, taking on an asymmetric shape as a result of a shift in frequency that is equivalent in magnitude to the natural width of a specific atomic transition in strontium. This effect becomes more pronounced under conditions of high saturation. Our research incorporated momentum transfers resulting from the absorption and emission of photons, as described by a modified version of the optical Bloch equations. We demonstrated that even a single-beam setup can illustrate photon recoil effects that have substantial implications for fields like saturation spectroscopy, Ramsey interferometry, and absorption imaging. Furthermore, we showed that the shape of the absorption profile can be utilized to measure the velocity distribution of ultracold gases with improved precision. For example, in the case of a cloud of 10,000 atoms at a temperature of 100 nK, the velocity distribution's standard deviation can be resolved with an accuracy of 0.13 mm/s, significantly enhancing the capability to evaluate atomic velocities in ultracold systems. Our findings are particularly relevant to the strontium atom, a crucial element in the creation of ultracold molecules, but the principles we discovered are equally applicable to other ultracold gas systems. Overall, our research highlighted an often-overlooked aspect of light-atom interactions that can offer valuable insights and accurate measurements in ultracold gas experiments. Our approach can be adapted for other situations and systems involving strong coupling between light and matter. Additionally, we observed an anomaly in the absorption pattern that is thought to be caused by a non-ideal counterpropagation configuration, which could be useful for detecting the effects of counterpropagation on atom-light interactions in one-dimensional systems. When subjected to high stresses, the vast majority of dense mixtures undergo a sudden and extreme thickening, characterized by a transition from fluid-like behavior to rigidity. Researchers propose that abrupt shear thickening serves as an initial indicator of a state transition, developing a comprehensive framework for interpreting viscosity through a universal function that bridges the frictionless point of jamming and a state of rigidity influenced by friction, anisotropy, and shear. Studies involving cornstarch in glycerol and silica spheres in glycerol found that for these two systems, viscosity can be condensed into a singular, stress- and volume fraction-independent curve, revealing distinct scaling regimes that reflect different universality classes and implying that isotropic and anisotropic shear jamming have unique characteristics. Furthermore, by integrating the effects of microscale interactions into a dimensionless variable that gauges the distance from shear jamming, scientists have paved the way for applying theories developed for equilibrium phenomena to better understand the physics governing the shear thickening transition. Ultimately, this work lays the groundwork for a unified understanding of the complex interactions governing fluid-like and rigid-like states of matter in the context of shear stress.

An area where Web search personalisation's effect on professional work has been inadequately studied is that of professional knowledge work on the Web. This study examines public sector officials' reliance on Google's Web search engine for their assessment, their knowledge of potential biases in search algorithms and the influence they have on retrieving all relevant information. The study's results show that a substantial number of the participants are unaware of potential biases in search algorithms and the possible strategies to prevent them from overlooking essential information. Notably, our data reveal that as much as 20% of the necessary information may go undetected due to the influence of Web search personalisation. This study's findings highlight the significance of Web search for public sector professionals, suggesting the necessity for training on search algorithms' potential biases that can shape judgments and decisions. In addition, it is crucial that these professionals are provided with guidelines to reduce the likelihood of missing relevant information. This study's implications for the public sector's reliance on Web search professional development and potential policy interventions are discussed. Furthermore, it presents a framework for evaluating search-based knowledge work that is subject to bias and provides a roadmap for future research in this area. In summary, it is essential to explore the relationship between Web search personalisation and professional judgment to ensure that public sector professionals who use search engines are aware of the potential biases that may influence their assessments and decisions. In the end, this study encourages a more comprehensive examination of search-based knowledge work's ethical implications to ensure that search algorithms accurately support rather than distort professional knowledge and judgment. In the context of Google's search engine, it is particularly crucial to explore these implications given its dominance of the search engine market. We are suggesting the establishment of a state-of-the-art muon-proton and muon-nucleus collider that operates at the TeV level, capable of delivering highly accurate measurements in deep inelastic scattering in new areas, while also offering a comprehensive research agenda in particle and nuclear physics. By doing so, we believe it could either drive the advancement or make use of existing particle accelerators, specifically taking advantage of established infrastructure if constructed at places like Brookhaven National Laboratory, Fermilab, or CERN. In this concept, we outline various design parameters for several collider configurations and evaluate potential for scientific discoveries with studies on deep inelastic scattering processes, Higgs boson and vector boson production, top quark creation, and leptoquark beyond Standard Model. Additionally, considerations for detector designs and potential paths to realization are also discussed. Lastly, considering factors like energy reach, scientific scope, and implementation difficulties, we propose two initial research initiatives that could serve as building blocks for a fully-fledged muon collider. We are advocating for the creation of such a collider, confident it will serve a significant purpose in the future of particle and nuclear physics. A novel approach is proposed to create and assess a respiratory motion-compensated four-dimensional T2-weighted MRI sequence, which is crucial in radiology and radiotherapy treatments guided by MRI. Data acquisition is continuous via a spiral acquisition method with reordering of Cartesian sampling points (rCASPR) that ensures matching image contrast and sorts data into respiratory phases. Initial 4D images are reconstructed using a compressed sensing technique and deformation fields are estimated for compensation in subsequent images. Experiments with phantom and human subjects compared sampling methods, including in silico trials. Parameters for low-resolution reconstruction, including resolution and regularization, were optimally selected through a grid search method. Motion compensation in rCASPR was tested in eight subjects with results indicating better point-spread-function in rCASPR with little difference in contrast, thus making it feasible for direct application in radiology and radiotherapy treatments. Optimized 4D MRI reconstruction parameters were also determined with spatial resolution and temporal regularization set at $4.5mm^3$ and $10^{-4}$. A quantitative evaluation of image quality through the use of gradient entropy showed a score of 22.02 for motion-compensated rCASPR. Ultimately, this rCASPR-based method provides high-quality, free-breathing MRI images that minimize alterations in scan duration and image contrast, allowing direct application in radiology and radiotherapy treatments guided by MRI. The paired-permutation test in NLP systems has long relied on testing the statistical significance of differences in performance. This test aims to verify that observed discrepancies aren't simply coincidental. Despite the importance of accurate results, a lack of suitable exact algorithms forces practitioners to use time-consuming Monte Carlo approximations to achieve this goal. In contrast, we've developed an efficient method for calculating paired-permutation test results exactly. This exact algorithm takes significantly less time to compute than Monte Carlo methods. In particular, we observed a 10 times speedup when using our exact algorithm versus the commonly employed Monte Carlo approximation on a representative dataset of 20000 samples. Moreover, we've made the paired-permutation test exact without incurring a notable increase in computational costs for other common tests, such as the paired t-test and confidence interval construction, by leveraging the same algorithmic framework. We've also included exact implementations of the paired t-test and bias-corrected confidence interval in our package, which is available openly for use by the community. We've conducted extensive testing to ensure the robustness and precision of these implementations, and we've tested the paired-permutation test exact algorithm on multiple real-world datasets and use cases. We've found that using exact paired-permutation tests leads to a 5-10% increase in test rejection rates in certain scenarios. We've made our code publicly accessible for others to use and modify as needed. Furthermore, we've created an interactive visualizer to demonstrate the performance of the paired-permutation test exact algorithm graphically. We've also contributed our paired-permutation test exact algorithm to the scikit-learn library, which is a widely used, comprehensive machine learning library in Python. We've written a detailed guide on how to use the paired-permutation test exact algorithm effectively in practice, and we've explored various aspects of its performance in depth. We've found that using exact paired-permutation tests leads to more reliable and precise results, and we recommend using these exact tests in place of Monte Carlo approximations in NLP systems. We've conducted thorough testing to ensure the precision and robustness of our implementations, and we've made our code and accompanying data freely available for the community to use and build upon.
