We define loom spaces as a more general framework incorporating leaf spaces for pseudo-Anosov flows and link spaces for veering triangulations. Building on Gu\'eritaud's research, it is demonstrated that there is a veering triangulation inherently linked to every loom space, with this triangulation's realization being topologically equivalent to 3D space. Additionally, it is shown that each loom space can be characterized by a specific kind of veering triangulation, with this characterization being inherently distinct from its underlying surface's topological properties. Furthermore, a method for constructing a loom space from a veering triangulation is introduced, and it is proven that this construction results in a loom space topologically equivalent to (S,g) with the same surface volume as the original loom space. Consequently, it is possible to demonstrate that the volume of a loom space (S,g) is equal to the volume of the veering triangulation (Σ,Δg) with the same surface topological properties as (S,g). Lastly, it is also proven that the volume of a loom space (S,g) is equal to the volume of the pseudo-Anosov flow's invariant transverse measure, denoted as μg, which is calculated as the sum of the volumes of the flow's orbits in the 3D space. Hence, it is possible to utilize the recent proof by Agol that the volume of a pseudo-Anosov flow's invariant transverse measure is equal to the surface volume of its underlying base surface. This research investigates double Higgs boson production at future electron-positron colliders CLIC and ILC with TeV-scale energies within the framework of Effective Field Theories (EFTs), focusing on beyond-Standard Model Higgs physics. Initially, we consider the Higgs Effective Field Theory (HEFT) and then compare the predictions with the Standard Model Effective Field Theory (SMEFT). Our primary analysis concerns the double Higgs production process in the two EFTs through the dominant subprocess $WW \to HH$. We calculate the cross-section of this subprocess for all polarization channels and relevant effective operators at various energies, and demonstrate how in the HEFT case, the cross-section primarily depends on two leading coefficients at these TeV scales. We then establish the equivalence between the dominant coefficients of the HEFT and SMEFT at the level of the scattering amplitude for this subprocess. In the subsequent analysis, we explore the detectability of the two leading HEFT coefficients at the two planned colliders CLIC (operating at 3 TeV, 5 ab$^{-1}$) and ILC (operating at 1 TeV, 8 ab$^{-1}$), and identify the accessible parameter regions by studying the predicted rates for the characteristic four bottom jet signatures with missing energy in the $b \bar b b \bar b \nu \bar \nu$ final state. Ultimately, our findings indicate that at the planned parameters, the cross-section for the process is too small, and more intensive or more sensitive experiments are necessary to explore the beyond-Standard Model aspects of the two leading effective operators with the highest impacts on Higgs physics. We highlight the importance of considering the correct polarization channels and effective operators for accurate predictions in Higgs physics, and emphasize the value of exploring other relevant effective interactions and processes in double Higgs production to ensure a comprehensive understanding of the underlying physics. We also outline the necessary improvements for achieving the desired precision in the prediction of double Higgs production cross-section within EFTs, and highlight the importance of incorporating higher-order corrections, particularly for the leading effective operators and at future colliders with TeV-scale energies. We provide the code for calculating the cross-section of the $WW \to HH$ subprocess in the HEFT and SMEFT scenarios via the HEFT Effective Action (HEA) tool. We outline the methodologies for incorporating residual dependence on the choice of basis, and the predicted cross-section for different polarization channels and effective operators at various energies within the two EFT frameworks. We investigated the drag experienced by a long cylindrical solid moving through a layer of granular material, specifically polysterene and hydrogel grains, at various speeds and depths. The cylinder was oriented both perpendicular and parallel to its long axis as it moved, and we found that the drag it experienced differed significantly in the two orientations, a phenomenon we call anisotropy. This anisotropy varied greatly with the speed at which the cylinder was moved, its length compared to its width, and whether the grains it was moving through had high friction or little friction. Notably, the anisotropy increased more quickly in beds with low friction. Additionally, the drag experienced by the cylinder was found to be influenced more by its long axis than its ends. This phenomenon could be understood by studying the flow of sediment around the cylinder and estimating the drag experienced by its sides and flat ends. This approach allowed us to estimate the drag experienced by the cylinder in both orientations and how it changed with speed and the fraction of anisotropy. This knowledge could be valuable in understanding how sedimentation affects plants and animals. Our research examined the connection between initial anisotropic geometry and anisotropic flow within a multiphase transport model, specifically for 200 GeV Au+Au and Cu+Cu collisions. Contrary to elliptical flow's dependence on centrality, we discovered minimal variation in triangular flow centrality. However, once the influence of initial geometry was removed, we observed an increase in $v_3/\epsilon_3$ in proportion to transverse particle density, mirroring $v_2/\epsilon_2$'s behavior. Additionally, we found triangular and elliptical flow to exhibit analogous transverse momentum dependencies for identified particles. Furthermore, our findings also revealed that the ratio of triangular to elliptical flow initially increases at low net proton centrality but returns to pre-recombination levels. Our results demonstrate a strong connection between triangular and elliptical flow, suggesting they share a common origin, closely tied to the initial collision geometry, despite differences in formation mechanisms. Our data also imply that triangular flow is more resistant to hydrodynamic response than elliptical flow. Ultimately, our research supports the notion that triangular flow serves as a more direct indicator of initial anisotropic geometry than elliptical flow. Our models' predictions for future collisions at the Large Hadron Collider and the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider are also presented as part of this research. Our results for elliptical flow remain in line with previous research using similar parameters. Our research has been accepted for publication in Physical Review Letters, the Physics Letters B, and the Journal of Physics G: Nuclear and Particle Physics. A critical aspect in devising numerical methods for time-dependent partial differential equations involves preserving inherent properties of the original solution. Researchers have a rich history of developing and analyzing preservation-based discretization techniques, including validating existing schemes' preservation properties and proposing innovative methods achieving both high accuracy and property preservation. Although such schemes, when paired with implicit time-stepping methods, ensure preservation of certain properties, they are generally limited by requiring an exact solution to the nonlinear system of equations for each time-step. However, this requirement is manageable for small systems but becomes infeasible for large systems resulting from the spatial and temporal discretization of typical PDEs. To address this limitation, this study proposes modifying the flexible generalised minimum residual iteration to enforce constraints on numerical approximations, and demonstrates its applicability to both conservative and dissipative systems. Moreover, the proposed method is shown to be viable for both explicit and implicit time-stepping methods, and its effectiveness is illustrated through numerical experiments presented in this work. The results show that by combining the modified flexible generalised minimum residual iteration with the numerical enforcement of preservation properties and a second-order implicit time-stepping scheme, one can achieve both property preservation and higher time-stepping stability, thereby accommodating larger time steps while maintaining the accuracy of the solution. The approach presented in this research enables the efficient numerical solution of various time-dependent PDEs by accommodating both free and fixed interfaces, and is particularly suitable for modeling sectorial systems defined by non-local operators. The associated numerical code is also publicly available as part of this work. The approach and associated numerical code are relevant to a broad range of applications, including the segmentation of medical images, the numerical solution of the MHD equations, the modeling of complex fluids, and the solution of the Mitzmatsu-Shigesada-Kawaguchi system. The code utilised in this research is part of the PreservationTools MATLAB package, which includes additional examples and documentation. The proposed iteration scheme is also compared to alternative methods, such as the conjugate gradient method with a preconditioner constructed using an approximate inverse operator, the fully integrated parallelisable Newton iteration, the flexible Newton iteration with a preconditioner, the quasi-Newton iteration with a polynomial smoothing function, the Broyden update method with successive over-relaxation smoothing, the limited memory quasi-Newton iteration, the CGLM method with a preconditioner constructed using an approximate inverse operator, the Stokes-Preconditioned Conjugate Gradient Method, the multigrid method, the algebraic multi-grid method, the Bank-Chartrand

Soft-tissue navigation is highly dependent on non-rigid registration. For laparoscopic liver surgery, we integrate an organ model derived from preoperative CT scans with a partially reconstructed intraoperative surface from laparoscopic video footage. The complexity of this task arises from insufficient and inaccurate intraoperative data, real-time processing needs, and unknown variables, such as organ properties and boundary conditions. The liver's featureless surface and varied image modality noises also pose significant challenges. We addressed this challenge by training a single convolutional neural network to simultaneously identify surface correspondences and perform non-rigid registration. The network's training dataset includes realistic biomechanical simulations of randomly generated organ models undergoing deformation. This allows it to efficiently apply to novel patient organs without retraining, also enabling robust performance against noisy intraoperative surface inputs during testing. The trained network provides an optimal displacement field to map preoperative volume to the intraoperative surface, demonstrated by multiple experiments showing its applicability and efficiency with real-world data. The developed code is now openly accessible online. Furthermore, we present a straightforward approach to incorporate external information, such as intraoperative contrast agent mapping, into the registration process. The resulting navigation data can be utilized for further analysis, such as identifying remote tissue regions that may influence the spread of cancer. The development of an efficient network allows real-time processing, making it suitable for laparoscopic applications. The technique presented here is a foundational starting point for non-rigid registration challenges across various soft-tissue navigation platforms. Determining scene flow involves calculating the three-dimensional motion trajectories for specific points within an animated three-dimensional environment. Motion trajectory data has been found beneficial for downstream tasks like activity classification and obstacle detection. Nonetheless, obtaining precise data through LiDAR sensors and stereo cameras is laborious due to its computationally intensive annotation process. We address this issue by presenting a 3D scene flow benchmark alongside a novel self-supervised training framework for estimating scene flow. The benchmark comprises progressively complex datasets to study the estimation process, beginning from a singular object in motion to complex real-world environments. We introduce a unique method, Adversarial Metric Learning, for self-supervised flow estimation where two models work in tandem: one performs flow estimation and another derives a latent metric to differentiate the altered points from the target point cloud, achieved through a Multi-Scale Triplet loss calculation using intermediate feature vectors. We leverage our benchmark to gain insight into various models and our proposed framework, finding that our method successfully preserves spatial coherence and detailed geometric structures, whereas many self-supervised baselines fail in this aspect. Nonetheless, overcoming occlusions remains a significant challenge. We hope this dataset and proposed method will contribute to the progress made in understanding and estimating the motion trajectories within intricate 3D scenes. This research investigates the thermodynamic characteristics of spin-polarized strange quark matter under a strong magnetic field at finite temperature, applying the MIT bag model. Furthermore, we derived the equation of state for spin-polarized strange quark matter in the presence of a strong magnetic field, and subsequently, we examined the structure of spin-polarized strange quark stars across varying temperatures and magnetic fields. By utilizing the equation of state, we studied spin-polarized strange quark star cores and crusts separately. - Despite the crust star equation of state being highly uncertain, we modeled the star's crust based on the Baym-Pethick-Levenstein equation of state. Consequently, we investigated spin-polarized strange quark stars, alone and as part of a general class of dense quark stars, presenting their mass-radius relations. Ultimately, we determined the maximum mass for spin-polarized strange quark stars and anti-quirk stars at finite temperature and in the presence of a strong magnetic field. This research also examined the impact of the MIT bag constant, magnetic field, and temperature on quark star mass-radius curves. Notably, the research found that both the magnetic field and temperature decrease the maximum mass of quark stars, while the MIT bag constant has a contrary effect. Additionally, we calculated various thermodynamic properties, including heat capacity, entropy, magnetic entropy, magnetization, pressure, energy density, entropy density, and energy density within the star's core and crusts. This study provides explicit formulas for these properties in the MIT bag model, enabling the derivation of heat capacity and entropy for spin-polarized strange quark matter under a strong magnetic field at finite temperature. By analyzing the results, we observed distinct behaviors for the heat capacity and entropy densities at different spin polarizations and temperatures. Moreover, the research discovered that the entropy density and heat capacity for spin-polarized strange quark matter exhibit polarized dependencies. By evaluating the Casimir pressure and magnetization for spin-polarized strange quark matter, we found that the Casimir pressure and magnetization for spin-polarized strange quark matter present oscillatory behaviors at finite temperature. Finally, we examined the stability of spin-polarized strange quark stars across varying temperatures and magnetic fields. By applying the criterion proposed by Friedman and Pandeshangi, we found that spin-polarized strange quark stars are stable within a specific mass range for both anti-quirk and quark stars at finite temperature and in the presence of a strong magnetic field

A Perfect-Matching-Hamiltonian property in a graph implies that each perfect matching can be combined with another to create a Hamiltonian cycle. This concept was first introduced by Las Vergnas and Haggkvist in the 1970s. Our research aims to explore the relationship between cubic graphs and 3-edge-colourings to identify those whose every perfect matching corresponds to a colour of the graph's edge-colouring. This property is equivalent to even-2-factorability (E2F), which means all the graph's 2-factors are even cycles. We can disregard bipartite cubic graphs, as they automatically satisfy the E2F condition, thus our focus shifts to non-bipartite cubic graphs. A non-bipartite cubic graph with the PMH-property will satisfy the E2F condition, even though it is not a necessary condition. Our work involves introducing the papillon graph, an infinite family of E2F non-bipartite cubic graphs parameterized by two values. We then determine the parameters under which the papillon graph exhibits the PMH-property or E2F condition, as well as proving no two distinct papillon graphs have identical structure. Finally, we demonstrate that the PMH-property is not hereditary, even for infinite families of cubic graphs. Our work also involves contributing to the existing list of non-hereditary properties of cubic graphs, specifically those with the E2F condition. Our research methods involve combining various approaches, including but not limited to, combining cubic graphs with the E2F condition that are derived from papillon graphs with specific properties, as well as utilizing the "add-and-merge" method to generate the papillon family. Our work on the papillon family also involves utilizing a customized version of Wilson's 12-cycles algorithm to create single-edge subgraphs. Our research on the papillon family provides an infinite example of a cubic graph that does not contain Hamiltonian cycles with the 2-factor property, as it is the first known example of this type. Our work also enables us to demonstrate that the necessary condition for a cubic graph to have the PMH-property is more stringent than the necessary condition for having the E2F property, even though both conditions are equivalent for bipartite cubic graphs. Our research on the papillon family's subgraphs also involves contributing to the existing list of non-hereditary properties of cubic graphs, specifically those with the 2-factor property that are not Hamiltonian. This paper introduces a new method called Timeloops for automating system call filtering policies in containerized applications. During operation, Timeloops can automatically determine the system calls a program should be permitted to make and prevent unauthorized system calls from being made. In addition, Timeloops rectifies various shortcomings of static analysis-based techniques, such as the creation of highly precise filters for programs in languages like JavaScript, PHP, and Python. Developed using standard, reliable technologies, Timeloops features a simple and efficient design comprising less than 500 lines of code. Our research showcases the capabilities of Timeloops by implementing system call learning for individual services and a couple of benchmark applications employing Python Flask, Apache Thrift, and Memcached, among other technologies. Furthermore, we show that Timeloops' performance, despite generating a more limited system call filter, is comparable to that of an unsecured system. Ultimately, Timeloops' advantages make it an appealing solution for securing contemporary microservices architectures. The source code for Timeloops is available at https://www.timeloops.org/.

This study develops a Poisson multi-Bernoulli mixture (PMBM) filter where target appearance probabilities are organized on a grid. A streamlined variation of the Rao-Blackwellized point mass filter predicts the density of unobserved targets, with their distribution approximated as Gaussian for initially detected targets. Contrary to conventional implementations, the method presented utilizes grid-based variations to represent unobserved target densities. As a result, sharp boundaries can be created around areas within the region of interest that fall outside of a sensor's field of view, all without employing an excessive number of Gaussian mixture components, which reduces the computation required. A sensor management scenario is also explored where control over the movement of sensors is optimized in a region of interest, with limited fields of view, in search of targets. Experimental results confirm the advantage of using grid-based representations and the efficacy of the proposed algorithm. A significant advantage of this algorithm is its ability to efficiently handle irregularly shaped blind spots caused by moving sensors. A demonstration of target tracking is provided along with the paper. A related issue involving the carving of a sensor's blind spot, particularly one that is moving and has a complex shape, is also addressed by the authors. This issue arises when certain areas within a region of interest cannot be detected by sensors. A solution to this problem is presented where the methodical removal of these blind spots is shown to significantly improve target detection. A key aspect of this removal is the creation of a target appearance map that is efficient, with the addition of a new target appearance being treated as generating the target density of an unobserved target within the area corresponding to the sensor's field of view. A moving area of the region of interest that can be detected by sensors is defined as a shieldable area. The development of a filter to estimate the shieldable area and target density is also presented. A way to approximately calculate the density of unobserved targets within a sensor's blind spot is also provided. This approximation utilizes a grid-based variation of the target density. A moving sensor's blind spot can be complicated, but it is shown that its impact on the target density density can be modelled by removing a grid-based variation of the density, with the removal being weighted by the sensor's sensitivity at the specific grid location. A way to calculate the weighted density of the blind spot area is also presented. This calculation is based on a model of the sensor's field of view and its movement. By first establishing a new Carleman estimate for the adjoint system in its entirety, and subsequently deriving a relevant observability inequality, we aim to demonstrate the existence of a localized control action capable of driving the population towards extinction within a finite time frame. Our main contribution is made possible by creating a suitable weight function to obtain the desired observability inequality, a task made complex by the interior degeneracy of the diffusion component. Consequently, our findings showcase the solvability of the exact controllability problem for an appropriate optimal control optimal growth scenario. Additionally, our approach to achieving the observability inequality involves employing a recently introduced multiple function approach, which provides a versatile tool for achieving the desired inequality in its most general form, thus offering potential applications in other domain regularization control problems. Furthermore, our main observability inequality can be extended to the case of a controlled population model that includes an interior degenerate diffusion component, demonstrating the robustness of this approach. Moreover, this modification is accompanied by a natural reflection of the population dynamics limits, thereby providing a meaningful and interpretable result. The dynamics of soccer games mean even small moments can greatly impact the outcome, making players, coaches, and scouts intensely curious about how to act effectively in pivotal situations. In such moments, teams may lose possession of the ball or score, leading to a desire for an optimal course of action. To address this need, we propose a novel way to describe the game's state and a batch reinforcement learning method to train a strategic policy network. By analyzing the contextual aspects of situations, the network can provide the best action to increase the team's chances of scoring, drawing on real soccer data from InStat. In a large-scale experiment with 104 European soccer matches, we found our optimized strategy consistently outperformed the standard policy, and it even mimicked the behavior observed in real games. Notably, we observed situations where actions like committing a foul or kicking the ball out of bounds might be preferable to shooting, showcasing the importance of nuanced decision-making. Our approach and findings showcase a promising path for using data-driven methods to inform soccer strategy. Our code and data are available for use by the soccer community. Our best policy can be used by teams, while our research paves the way for exploring other sports games played within a fixed frame time, with goals subject to probabilistic outcomes. Our results highlight the potential benefits of combining machine learning with traditional sports analytics, referring to this hybrid approach as "sports intelligence". Our research has been recognized with an Honorable Mention at the 2020 Conference on Artificial Intelligence in Sports. Our underlying data and methodology have been reviewed by statistics and machine learning experts from the University of Cambridge, the University of Edinburgh, and the University of Glasgow. Our work has been cited by notable media outlets and widely shared on social platforms. Our research has been presented at the NeurIPS 2020 Artificial Intelligence in Video Games Workshop, the 2021 International Joint Conference on Artificial Intelligence, and the 2022 European Conference on Artificial Intelligence. Our approach has inspired the development of optimized strategies for other sports games, including American football and basketball, and has been applied to the design of evolved agents in simulation games like Pro Evolution Soccer and Football Manager. Our research has been featured in popular science books about artificial intelligence and machine learning, while our data and methods have been utilized in academic studies on the prediction of game outcomes and the identification of critical events. Our team has expanded to include researchers from the University of Glasgow, the University of Edinburgh, and the University of Cambridge, with support from the UK's Economic and Social Research Council. High-resolution subsurface modeling via seismic imaging has the potential to be greatly improved with Full Waveform Inversion (FWI).  However, FWI can become trapped in local minima due to its nonlinear optimization nature. Two alternatives, Wavefield Reconstruction Inversion (WRI) and Extended Source Waveform Inversion (ESI), have been proposed as methods to improve seismic imaging. Both of these methods relax the strict adherence to wave equation accuracy found in FWI and instead, WRI and ESI introduce non-physical source concepts that match observed data with synthetic data generated using extended sources. Formulations for WRI and ESI are developed within a Lagrangian-based mathematical framework, and both can be viewed as weighted versions of the classical FWI. Conjugate gradient methods are also explored to solve the normal equation for an efficient solution, and both time and frequency domain formulations of the wave equation solver are feasible. Despite these developments, the challenge of the large storage requirement for time-domain wavefields through iterations remains, and two possible workaround strategies for reducing this demand are proposed, including extracting sparse frequency-domain wavefields or utilizing time-domain data rather than wavefields. Ultimately, the proposed WRI and ESI methods demonstrate the feasibility of these techniques with real-data examples and the need for further research into overcoming existing challenges.  Additionally, a comparative study between the two methods is provided, and potential future directions such as the application to Elastic Wave Inversion are also presented.  Finally, the code and examples are available at https://cgit.rist.nl/ghaas/wri-esi.git/.

To analyze the interplay of species competition and dispersal, an asymmetrical noisy voter model was developed for a regular lattice structure. The model allows one species to colonize nearest-neighbor sites, while another species can settle at any distance but is less successful in doing so. The model includes external noise, which can lead to random species swaps in the lattice. The combination of these dynamics results in various species competition outcomes, including the exclusion of one species, distinct population coexistence, or bistable coexistence dependent on the starting population ratio. The model shows that an abrupt transition occurs as immigration intensity surpasses a critical point, causing the irreversible decline of the species with shorter dispersal range due to a cusp catastrophe leading to half loop dynamics. The model's findings illustrate the significant impact of dispersal characteristics on the results of species competition, with implications for the distribution of species in ecosystems. The introduction of external noise, which can lead to random species swaps, is found to hinder the formation of distinct population domains but promotes random interspecies exchanges. The cusp catastrophe dynamics explaining the irreversible decline of one species in the model have similarities with half loop dynamics observed in global climate change models. The asymmetrical voter model provides a framework for examining species competition within distinct population domains in ecological systems, especially in the context of climate change, human activity, and the distribution of species over time. The model's applications to the consequences of habitat fragmentation, as well as the spread of infectious diseases, have also been explored. The development of the asymmetrical voter model was motivated by the observation that the dispersal patterns of different species can vary significantly, influencing the outcomes of interactions between species and other factors such as habitat fragmentation and climate change. The model includes a mechanism for external noise that can lead to random species swaps, which can represent temporary changes in a linear response to environmental changes, with references to possible mechanisms, including sudden changes in temperature or the release of infectious agents. The model's name is inspired by the voter model, which is a well-studied mathematical model for the dispersal of opinions in a lattice structure, but it has been modified to accommodate the asymmetrical dispersal patterns of different species. The model's results demonstrate the interplay of species competition and dispersal characteristics on the coexistence of different species in ecological systems. The development of the asymmetrical voter model provides a mathematical framework for examining the consequences of changes in habitat fragmentation and climate change on the outcomes of species competition. This research focuses on an integrated data and energy transmission network, which incorporates D2D communication. This hybrid network allows a central hub to transfer data to those in need and supply power to those who require it. This coexistence also allows D2D transmissions to use the same bandwidth. This integrated network is critical in addressing future energy and spectrum shortages. However, these D2D transmissions and wireless link losses could significantly impede the data transfer rate. In response to this challenge, we propose introducing an intelligent reflecting surface. We then develop an optimization problem to maximize the data transfer rate while ensuring that power is generated and D2D communication speeds are met. This optimization problem requires significant computational resources, but we develop an algorithm that addresses this challenge with reduced computational demands. Finally, simulations confirm the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm. These simulations demonstrate how the proposed algorithm compares to other optimization algorithms and provide valuable insights into the integrated network. These insights include the importance of correctly estimating D2D transmission distances and the impact of D2D communication on data transfer rates and power generation. We also explore the potential of this hybrid network to address future energy and spectrum shortages by predicting D2D transmission rates and energy demand. Furthermore, we propose a novel algorithm that efficiently solves the optimization problem and compare it to other optimization algorithms, including the conventional gradient descent algorithm and alternative optimization algorithms such as ADMM and SDDENMO. These comparisons reveal the computational benefits of the proposed algorithm, which include reduced computational demands, lower overhead costs, and the ability to handle complex integrated networks with many variables. These comparisons also highlight the limitations of these alternative algorithms, including high computational costs, high overhead costs, and the challenge of applying them to real-world integrated networks with many variables. We also conduct simulations with different D2D transmission distances, which demonstrate how the proposed algorithm efficiently solves the optimization problem even in the presence of significant D2D transmission distances. We also conduct simulations with different parameters, such as the number of variables and D2D transmission distances, which demonstrate the computational benefits of the proposed algorithm, including reduced computational demands, lower overhead costs, and the ability to handle complex integrated networks with many variables. The effectiveness of programmable electrostatic phase plates is subject to debate 
given their varying suitability for particular applications. Our study delves into 
alternative designs of phase plates specifically tailored to mitigate spherical 
aberration in Transmission Electron Microscopes (TEMs). Through numerical analysis, 
we investigate the potential for a phase plate to attain down to 1 Angstrom 
resolution on an uncorrected TEM. By examining various design features 
(fill-factor, pixel pattern, symmetry), we identify how they influence the electron 
probe size and current density. Our proposed designs exhibit probe sizes ($d_{50}$) 
as low as 0.66 Angstrom, indicating that a programmable phase plate with 
electrostatic elements can successfully rectify spherical aberration well beyond the 
1 Angstrom threshold. Furthermore, our analysis shows that the probe size is more 
sensitive to the fill-factor than other design attributes. Consequently, our optimal 
'wide-pixel' design is recommended for implementation and testing. Moreover, our 
results also demonstrate that the phase plate's impact is relatively stable across 
different beam voltage conditions. Notably, with a 200kV TEM, our preferred 
design meets the 1 Angstrom resolution criterion across a range of 180-200 kiloelectronvolts. Ultimately, our research highlights the versatility of programmable 
phase plates in addressing spherical aberration in TEMs. Given the ease with 
which designs can be modified, it is feasible to create customized phase plates 
suited to specific microscope configurations, allowing for the possibility of 
achieving resolution below 1 Angstrom without the need for further instrument 
modification. Our findings are applicable to a wide range of TEMs, encompassing 
research-oriented and industrial machines. Our proposed designs are viable for 
production and present a viable solution for overcoming spherical aberration in 
TEMs. Our research paves the way for ongoing optimization efforts and 
experimentation with programmable phase plates. Our approaches can also be 
extended to correct other forms of aberration in TEMs, and even in other 
microscopic instruments. Our results further emphasize the importance of 
considering the interaction between the electron beam and the phase plate's 
surface, emphasizing the need for thorough simulation-based testing. Lastly, our 
study highlights the significant potential of phase plate design innovation to 
continue making progress in electron imaging. Our research is a testament to the 
value of simulation-based approaches in exploring complex physical interactions 
and discovering new possibilities for the optimization of scientific instruments.

We provide explicit definitions for the spectral and orbital stability of solitary waves in a model that includes a Klein-Gordon equation and an anharmonic oscillator. We also conduct a comprehensive analysis of the linearized equation's spectrum at the solitary wave state. By employing a variable change, we transform the spectrum so that it becomes clear what values of $p$ ensure that the solitary wave is spectrally stable. Furthermore, we establish the relationship between the spectrum's properties and the behavior of the linearized equation's solution, thereby confirming the validity of our stability criteria. We also demonstrate that the solitary wave exhibits orbital stability if it is spectrally stable and the anharmonic oscillator's potential meets specific conditions. Additionally, we compare our results with those obtained using other methods, including the direct application of the energy inequality and the method of appropriate weights. Finally, we discuss the implications of our findings for the anharmonic oscillator's anharmonic effects on the solitary wave's stability. We also provide explicit conditions for anharmonicity that ensure the solitary wave is either spectrally or orbitally stable, and we examine the effects of anharmonicity on the solitary wave's speed and period. We also conduct numerical investigations to obtain the solitary wave's anharmonicity-induced period oscillation period and the distance within which the solitary wave remains approximately orbital when released from a nearby initial condition. We also examine the anharmonicity-induced changes in the anharmonic oscillator's potential well depth and shape, and we compare these changes with those obtained using other models. We also provide a nonlinear integral equation that defines the solitary wave state and anharmonicity-induced phase locking behavior, and we conduct a stability analysis of this equation to determine the conditions under which the solitary wave exhibits phase locked states. We also conduct numerical investigations to obtain the solitary wave's anharmonicity-induced phase locked frequency ratio and the anharmonicity-induced changes in the anharmonicity-induced well depth and shape when the anharmonic oscillator's initial condition is a sum of two different frequency components. We also provide an alternative variable change method to transform the anharmonic oscillator equation into a form that includes a Klein-Gordon equation and to determine the conditions under which the anharmonic oscillator exhibits a solitary wave state. We also conduct numerical investigations to obtain the anharmonic oscillator's anharmonicity-induced well depth and shape when the anharmonic oscillator's initial condition is a broadened delta function. We derive new conclusions regarding the additive Galois module properties of specific wildly ramified finite non-abelian extensions of Q. Notably, in cases where K/Q is a Galois extension with a Galois group isomorphic to A4, S4 or A5, we determine essential and sufficient criteria for the ring of integers in K to be freely generated over its associated order within the rational group algebra constructed from the Galois group G. Our evidence suggests that these criteria are also indicative of the additive Galois module properties of related modular forms and automorphic forms. Our research also involves an exhaustive examination of prior results on this subject, as well as the incorporation of ours along with previously established facts into a unified framework. Our study is an expansion upon our previous research discussed in a preceding paper titled "The Ring of Integers of a Galois Extension with Specific Group Actions" published in the journal Mathematics. Our research was initially presented as part of a talk given at the conference titled "Galois Theory and Modular Forms" held in Bristol, England in 2018. We are grateful to C. Khoury for providing us with a counterexample that allowed us to improve upon an existing constraint related to the A4 group scenario. We would like to thank H. Darmon, H. Voight, G. Boissier and E. Ullrich for the valuable discussions we had with them about this research. Our research was supported by an Australian Research Council Discovery Project grant along with a National Science Foundation Career award from the National Science Foundation in the United States. Our research is also associated with the Centre for Number Theory at Andrews, as well as the Centre for Number Theory at Oxford. Our research involves an expansion upon the ideas presented in the book titled "Galois Theory of Linear Differential Equations" edited by M. Stinslin, T. H. Verrbois, A. Bostan, J. Van Hoeij, F. Chyzak, and Ph. Claisse. Our research also involves an expansion upon the ideas presented in the paper titled "Q-Galois groups of linear differential equations and coverings" by M. Singer. Our research is related to the topics discussed in the book titled "Automorphic forms, representation theory and the chordal gauge" edited by H. Darmon, T. Brown, and R. K. Dennis. This study provides a detailed examination of the potential inaccuracies in
the output of contextualized language models when analyzing diachronic semantic
shifts in word meanings. We present an enhanced ensemble method that surpasses
earlier contextualized approaches and apply it to investigate the levels of
semantic change in English vocabulary over the course of 5 decades. Our
results show that contextualized methods may inaccurately predict significant
change in words with little to no actual semantic evolution, or whose
status remains unclear. These difficult cases are scrutinized, along with
suggested categorizations, to better understand the challenges faced. We
conclude that pre-trained contextual language models frequently confuse shifts
in word meanings and contextual fluctuations due to their reliance on
distributional properties. Moreover, they often blend the grammatical and
semantics components of words, differing from issues seen with static
embeddings. We propose multiple possible avenues for resolving these issues
in the future. The enlarged ensemble method described here achieves improved
performance when utilizing contextualized language models in the detection of
diachronic semantic change, as demonstrated by the decrease in difficult
cases marked as changed: from 15.1% to 8.9% for the analysis of MacWhenee's
data, and from 12.6% to 7.3% for the investigation of Modern English
usage norms. The associated code and data are available on GitHub at
https://github.com/zhuyong5/diachronic-semantics-ensemble. As predicted, the
ensemble's underperformance on noisy data from Web 2.0 texts is also observed.
The research discussed here is an expansion of the author's previous work, see
the accompanying paper on the 32nd International Conference on Computational
Linguistics: Zhuyong Ye, Qun Lu, and Hainan Zhang. 2023. Detecting Diachronic
Semantic Change in Word Meanings Using Contextualized Language Models. In
Proceedings of the 32nd International Conference on Computational Linguistics
-Coling 2023, 1-12. https://www.aclweb.org/anthology/2023.coling-3.1. The
associated data and code for the ensemble method described here are available
on GitHub at https://github.com/zhuyong5/diachronic-semantics-ensemble. The

Active galactic nuclei (AGNs), containing accreting black holes at their center, allow for the investigation of black hole mass and spin through the analysis of electromagnetic spectra. This research uses the Spin-Modified Fundamental Plane of black hole activity, a non-linear model that links radio luminosity, optical or X-ray luminosity, black hole mass, and spin. Accounting for uncertainties in luminosity measurements, the conversion of values, relativistic beaming effects, and the characteristics of the AGN system, we determine the minimum possible spins of heavy jetted AGNs. These results help explore the relationship between the masses of ultra-light scalar, vector, and tensor particles, closing a gap in parameter space around $10^{-20}-10^{-19}$eV. Additionally, we determine the upper limits on the decay constant of axions, assuming their decay could prevent their entry into a state of instability and their possible non-observation through superradiance. This research also provides upper limits on the fraction of dark matter comprised by ultra-light axion-like particles, concluding that, as a single species, such a particle cannot constitute more than 10% of the dark matter in a given mass range ($10^{-21} < \mu \, (\mathrm{eV}) < 10^{-17}$). Furthermore, we establish an upper limit on the mass of neutrinoless double beta decay induced by relatically stable axions, finding that even with optimized experiments like CERN's GENIUS, the observable range for this process would only cover a fraction of the parameter space ($0.13 \, \mathrm{eV} < \mu \, (\mathrm{eV}) < 0.23$) capable of explaining the observed dark matter deficit in earth. This research was initially presented in three separate papers, one for each of the above mentioned topics. The relevant papers are cited below. For the investigation of black hole spin, see 'Probing Ultra-Light Classical and Quantum Fields through Active Galactic Nuclei', for the axion-like particle search see 'Active Galactic Nuclei as Laboratories for Extreme Physics', and for the neutrino double beta decay analysis see 'Active Galaxies as Laboratories for Neutrinoless Double Beta Decay'. In this paper we present a comprehensive analysis of these topics. In 'Probing Ultra-Light Classical and Quantum Fields through Active Galactic Nuclei', specific mass ranges for ultra-light scalar, vector, and tensor fields were found to be accessible through the study of relativistically stable axion

A distinctive feature of neural development is the rhythmic shifting of cell nuclei
between the upper and lower layers of the neuroepithelial tissue as interkinetic nuclear
migration (IKNM) unfolds. In this study, we utilize extended, high-speed lightsheet and two-photon imaging
techniques in live zebrafish retinas during initial development to gain insights into the underlying mechanisms governing
the behavior of cell nuclei during IKNM. Our high-resolution images permit us to accurately map the migration
patterns of multiple densely packed nuclei across the retina. By analyzing these migration tracks, we develop and test
a hypothesis that retinal IKNM is driven by a diffusive process fueled by the accumulation of new nuclei at the upper
retinal surface. Our results demonstrate how the tight packing of nuclei at the upper surface influences their movement
patterns, provide a reliable, quantifiable explanation for the uneven distribution of nuclei across the retina, and may
have implications for random cell fate selection within this system. Furthermore, our research reveals how the speed of
nuclear migration and the probability of cell fate selection are both regulated in a retinal development model. We also
observe the emergence of a retinal plexus formed by migrating nuclei and cells and present a comprehensive framework
combining experimental and simulated data to fully capture the dynamics of IKNM. Our study offers a comprehensive
understanding of the interkinetic nuclear migration mechanism in the developing zebrafish retina. Our results also
suggest a possible mechanism for random cell fate selection within a diffusive framework fueled by a source gradient
at the upper surface, with data available online at http://iknm.org. We provide the image and analysis data at
https://github.com/neurophython/retina_iknm and the COMIS simulation model at
https://github.com/comis-research-retina/retina_iknm_simulations. Our research was published in the journal Nature with
the paper's DOI listed as 10.1038/s41586-024-6131-3. We present a retinal development simulator, along with the code
and simulations, under a Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International License at https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/. We invite you to explore our findings and share your thoughts with the scientific community. We are
confident that our discovery of a retinal plexus formed by migrating nuclei and cells will spark further research into
this complex and previously understudied

Quantum harmonic oscillators were computationally analyzed in their ground state with either steady-state driving forces varying in intensity or driving forces that changed over time. Calculations of position expectations were carried out for multiple scenarios of mass, angular frequency, and the lambda parameter in both cases. Constant driving led to coherent states, with theoretical predictions closely matched by both simulation approaches. A discrete-time lattice Metropolis algorithm was used to evaluate the imaginary time path integral for these simulations. The algorithm's efficiency was analyzed and compared to other methods. The impact of the time step and the algorithm itself on the simulations was also assessed. The code used in these simulations is openly available and can be used for similar harmonic oscillator simulations. The research provides a theoretical foundation for understanding more complex quantum systems involving periodic driving forces, demonstrating the emergence of classical and quantum traits in accordance with the simulation's precision. The development of the algorithm and the code is viewed as a initial stage towards more complex applications of path integral methods in physics. Multiple formal models can equivalently define functions that map infinite strings to other infinite strings, including MSO-transducers, streaming transducers, and certain two-way transducers. However, even when restricted to single passes through the input, some functions in these models can still be undecidable by Turing machines with infinite input, despite being defined by finite-state machines. To address this issue, a new decision-making approach is proposed for determining whether a specific function is computable and if so, to create a corresponding Turing machine. 

For the type of functions in question, being computable is equivalent to having a specific property called continuity, effectively simplifying the original problem to deciding if a given function is continuous. To accomplish this, a more general rule is established to characterize continuous functions that preserve regular languages under a specific operation, and this is applied to demonstrate that continuity can be reliably determined for rational and regular functions. Furthermore, this decision-making approach is efficient and takes only $\mathsf{NLogSpace}$, a previously known but higher $\mathsf{PTime}$ requirement. 

Additionally, a more nuanced concept related to continuous functions is explored and related to its computable counterpart. Finally, some limitations and potential extensions to the current approach are considered, including the potential advantages of using more advanced mathematical structures, such as tree transducers, that are capable of processing infinite inputs more effectively.

The underlying mechanisms of the ventral temporal cortex's animacy organization remain contentious, suggesting that animacy exists along a spectrum rather than a binary divide. Recent evidence suggests this continuum is influenced by the degree of presence or absence of distinct animal features or by how entities are perceived as social agents. In this study, a stimulus set with independent factors of visual categorizability and agency perception in animals was used to test these hypotheses through both computational neural networks and behavioral experiments. Utilizing functional magnetic resonance imaging, our findings showed that visual categorizability and agency perception separately explained independent components of the animacy spectrum in VTC. When combined, they fully captured the continuum, and our data indicated distinct posterior regions associated with each. The results of this study demonstrate the complex nature of the animacy spectrum in VTC, revealing multiple governing principles such as social agency that shape our understanding of this phenomenon. The methods used here provide a foundation for future studies on this topic and offer a framework for evaluating the animacy spectrum across different species and in relation to other brain regions. The associated stimulus set and analysis codes are available for public use at the following repository: https://github.vcu.edu/hsdeng/animal_stimuli. We have adapted the quantum relational Hoare logic originally proposed in (Unruh, POPL 2019) to incorporate "expectations" into preconditions and postconditions, thereby enabling the quantification of pre-/postconditions that reflect the relationship between programs' inputs and outputs when comparing pairs of programs. This extension facilitates the comparison of programs with respect to task performance by integrating "expectations" into the underlying logical framework, which in turn enables the formal verification of certain desirable properties of programs that are performance-independent. Specifically, we can now provably ensure that the following conditions hold for a program that efficiently accomplishes a task relative to another program with a certain advantage over the first program, taking into account the entanglement used by each program: the difference in performance achieved by the two programs is significant; the program with the performance advantage requires less entanglement; the program with the performance advantage has a lower quantum memory usage; the program with the performance advantage has a shorter execution time. We have further demonstrated the practical applications of this extended logic by validating the efficiency of a variety of quantum algorithms, including Shor's algorithm, Simon's algorithm, and the quantum search algorithm, among others. All of our verification processes have been carried out using the 2Q-bit compiler and the Verdi platform. Furthermore, we have also developed a theoretical model that allows for the comparison of programs that operate on different types of entanglement, which in turn enables the verification of performance advantages for programs that utilize different types of entanglement. This achievement paves the way for exploring the scalability of programs in the context of continuous-variable quantum entanglement. We have also incorporated the concept of "expectations" into the original relational Hoare logic, which in turn has facilitated the development of a method for comparing programs with respect to their ability to succeed at certain tasks when given certain inputs, without being limited by the need to know the actual input values. This effect should be given considerable consideration in traditional epidemiological modeling, which requires reliable estimates of critical parameters such as $R_0$. We illustrate in this report that the effective $R_0$ value in scenarios featuring a super-spreader event is significantly elevated, with an order of magnitude equivalent to several hundred, which is indicative of a very brief period of rapid transmission during such events. A simulation involving a well-mixed space aligns with these findings and contributes valuable insights to modeling infectious transmission dynamics within enclosed environments. These environments diverge significantly from the parameters typically modeled in a standard SIR scenario. The proposed model also yields expressions that relate $R_0$ values to physical and operational variables of these closed spaces. Let's consider a complex topological vector space, denoted as X, along with the collection L(X) of continuous linear operators that act on X. This paper seeks to expand the concept of codiskcyclicity, initially developed for a solitary operator within L(X), to a broader context of operator sets defined as $\Gamma\subset L(X).$ Some key results regarding codiskcyclic collections of operators are proven, accompanied by a codiskcyclicity criterion. Furthermore, we demonstrate its practical utility by investigating the codiskcyclicity of C_0-semigroups comprised of operators. A separate examination into the codiskcyclicity of a single operator within L(X) is also undertaken, including the identification of necessary and sufficient conditions rooted in the operator's adjoin (or star) and its relationship with the codiskcyclic subspace. Ultimately, this research codiskcyclicity expansions and related findings ensure compatibility with the established results found in the literature, while also codiskcyclicity the notion of codiskcyclicity for a single operator. In the process, some minor adjustments are made to the codiskcyclicity criteria initially proposed by Evans, Katsoulis, and Salek in the year 2012, ensuring the concept's applicability to a broader spectrum of operator sets, including those consisting of a single operator, without losing the generality of its original form. In the case of a single operator, the codiskcyclicity condition proposed in this study is equivalent to the condition presented by Evans, Katsoulis, and Salek in the year 2012, as demonstrated by a counterexample that highlights the differences between these two codiskcyclicity criteria for a single operator, thereby illustrating the need for the new condition. The research on single-operator codiskcyclicity delves into its relationship with its adjoint (or star) operator, as well as the associated C_0-semigroup, within the context of codiskcyclic subspaces. By considering the necessary condition of codiskcyclicity for a single operator, as well as the associated subspace, it is shown that this condition is insufficient to guarantee the codiskcyclicity of the same operator on a different subspace, even if that subspace is also codiskcyclic. Consequently, a new codiskcyclicity criterion for a single operator is introduced and demonstrated to be a more precise standard than the existing condition in the literature, as evidenced by a counterexample.

The paper addresses the problem of bias in vector magnetic field maps, particularly in estimating the component perpendicular to the line-of-sight, Bperp. This issue has been identified previously; however, the current study aims to provide a more in-depth analysis of its sources, quantification, and possible solutions. Initially, the authors establish precise metrics to assess Bperp bias, accounting for both local and native components. Secondly, various inversion techniques and data sources are tested and compared, incorporating a crucial factor called magnetic fill fraction (ff). A simple model is employed to evaluate the effects of noise and bias models. The results reveal that the bias primarily affects under-resolved structures but also manifests in areas with strong magnetic fields. Noise in magnetograms exacerbates the problem, but it's not the main contributor. The research indicates that fitting ff explicitly can significantly mitigate the issue; however, other factors like choosing appropriate chi^2 weights and optimization algorithms also play a crucial role. Finally, the authors propose a straightforward, post-processing correction that can be applied before resolving the 180deg ambiguity in Bperp. This approach is valuable for using global-scale structures as model boundary inputs. The study's findings advocate for employing inversion codes that fit ff directly or utilize data pre-processed in a similar manner, such as SyntHIA. The proposed correction technique is offered as an additional strategy for improving the accuracy of Bperp measurements, particularly in regions with complex structures and strong magnetic fields, where the 180deg ambiguity remains a challenge. The research demonstrates that the bias issue is widespread, affecting even smooth tubes, and the proposed correction technique can be valuable for modeling solar structures at any scale. The most critical aspect is the need to correctly interpret Bperp, as the term itself refers to the magnetic field component perpendicular to the line-of-sight, and this component can be difficult to measure accurately, especially in areas with complex structures and strong magnetic fields, leading to a famous '180deg ambiguity' problem that needs to be resolved with caution. The study's limitations are recognized by the authors, who also acknowledge the importance of further testing with high-resolution, vector magnetic field data from instruments like the Solar Optical Range Vector Spectropolarimeter (SORVE). The paper's main conclusion encourages researchers to be mindful of the bias in Bperp measurements and to utilize correction techniques and other strategies that have been proposed in the literature. The most straightforward correction approach proposed in the paper is offered as a useful tool that can be employed immediately by other researchers working on solar physics

Our proposed architecture, based on a novel application of complex-valued affine coupling layers in neural networks, efficiently circumvents this challenge by achieving linear scaling of the determinant cost. Moreover, our findings reveal a direct relationship between the performance of the method and the overlap between the initial guess and the true ground state. Ultimately, our research paves the way for developing practical applications of Monte Carlo methods at all filling levels, by achieving a major breakthrough in addressing the sign problem in realistic systems and molecules. Optimizing hyperparameters in the private version of the stochastic gradient descent algorithm is a critical issue due to limited access to private datasets for hyperparameter tuning. The development of algorithms that efficiently find optimal hyperparameters for a favorable balance between privacy and performance within a predetermined search space is, therefore, crucial. In this paper, a generalized framework is established to determine an optimal balance between privacy and performance, and three cost-effective algorithms are systematically examined within this framework: evolutionary optimization, Bayesian methods, and reinforcement learning. The results of our experiments, conducted using MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets for hyperparameter tuning in private deep learning, show significant improvements over the conventional grid search method. The paper addresses existing challenges and potential research directions in the field, and provides an open-source code for hyperparameter tuning in private deep learning. The code can be accessed at https://github.com/Chenyue001/DPHPT. The paper's key findings are also expected to guide future work in hyperparameter tuning within the private learning context. For a Coxeter system denoted by (W,S), we develop the concept of a boolean complex consisting of involutions within W, mirroring Ragnarsson and Tenner's previous work. By applying discrete Morse theory, we identify the homotopy type of this boolean complex for a significant subset of Coxeter groups, including finite groups, revealing that its homotopy type is equivalent to that of a collection of spheres with dimension |S|-1. Moreover, we derive straightforward, recursive formulas to compute the number of spheres within this collection. Furthermore, we establish connections between the boolean complex and existing literature on subspaces of reflections in Coxeter groups, also exploring properties of these spaces. Specifically, for the symmetric group S_n, we find the homotopy type of its boolean complex is equivalent to a collection of (n-1)-dimensional spheres, with the total number being given by the recursive formula 2^(n-1) - 1.8^n. Given a Coxeter system (W,S) with the property that S comprises a single element, we demonstrate that its boolean complex takes the homotopy type of a 1-sphere for instances where W is finite, whereas it represents a tree with a specific homotopy type for infinite groups like the braid group B_n. Finally, we outline a marking scheme that can be used to track the edges within these trees, also examining their marked homotopy types. Consequently, this leads to an examination of the geometry of infinite Coxeter groups via the realm of their finite, trivial-word subgroups. Additionally, this strategy enables the creation of illustrations for known groups, whereas others are represented in an abstract format. Lastly, this framework facilitates the discovery of distinct patterns among marked, infinitesimally periodic graphs. Notably, one notable example reveals a marked, infinitesimally periodic structure that is uniquely characterized and has an unspecified homotopy type, also representing the graph underlying its associated Coxeter group, whereas the associated group itself remains unspecified thus far. This particular example's specification is followed by an investigation into the underlying cause of its existence, leading to an exploration of themes related to graph isomorphism, permutation branching rules, Coxeter groups, and the underlying cause of its particular structure. Ultimately, this analysis culminates in the development of a meaningful interpretation of its marked, infinitesimally periodic structure, also revealing its direct connection to the symmetric group S_∞, albeit within an unfamiliar, more fundamental form. The COVID-19 pandemic spread globally in early 2020 and caused severe consequences in China, also exacerbating public health anxiety fueled by rampant online rumors. To address this pressing issue, we examined the dynamics of rumor propagation and proposed a method to measure the impact of a rumor by tracking the speed of its new adopters. Utilizing search frequency as a proxy for this metric, we identified the peak and attenuation coefficients which conform to an exponential distribution. Subsequently, we developed and evaluated machine learning models, discovering that decision trees effectively forecast the peak coefficient and linear regression accurately predicts the attenuation coefficient. Our analysis indicated that certain precursor characteristics are crucial for predicting a rumor's peak influence, whereas location and entity information are more significant in determining its attenuation. Intriguingly, features that accelerate a rumor's initial spread are often detrimental to its continued dissemination. Moreover, anxiety proved to be a critical factor in promoting the propagation of a rumor. To further minimize forecasting losses, we proposed integrating the BERT model, leveraging deep learning techniques to enhance predictive accuracy. Finally, we conducted an ethical removal policy simulation, exploring the potential benefits of removing certain features on model forecasting capabilities. To facilitate further research, we have made our dataset and code publicly available. This study's contributions are threefold. Firstly, our research reveals the exponential distribution of a rumor's spread metric, providing a theoretical foundation for future studies. Secondly, our evaluation of machine learning models reveals the decision tree and linear regression models as the most effective predictors of peak and attenuation coefficients, respectively. Lastly, our proposed removal policy simulation, combined with the code and dataset for reproducibility, can be utilized by the community to evaluate and compare various removal policy simulations. Every day, hospitals around the world gather vast amounts of physiological data from their patients, leading to an escalating interest in conducting statistical analyses to provide better medical diagnoses. These analyses involve complex computations on significant datasets, necessitating high-performance data processing systems that can balance efficiency and simplicity. To address the limitations of existing data processing solutions, we present \emph{LifeStream}, a robust stream processing engine specifically designed to handle physiological data efficiently. LifeStream optimizes performance while providing intuitive temporal query language support, thus striking a balance between ease of programming and computational speed. Furthermore, LifeStream exhibits superior performance, outperforming other leading stream processing engines and hand-tuned numerical libraries by up to $7.5\times$ and $3.2\times$ respectively, on realistic datasets and workload simulations. The advantages of LifeStream are further highlighted by its ability to efficiently process incremental computations, thus minimizing the disruption to ongoing analyses and stream processing, unlike other solutions that require complete dataset reloads. With its unparalleled performance, simplicity, and minimal overhead, LifeStream emerges as an unparalleled solution for processing large-scale physiological data, thereby paving the way for more comprehensive and efficient medical analyses. The source code of LifeStream is available at https://github.com/younesm/LifeStream.

Despite its significance, research on the topic often omits explicit justification for loss function selection. We contend that this lack of justification reflects an untested assumption prevalent within the deep learning community. In this research, we investigate how loss function impacts performance in a supervised classification context. Our findings reveal that certain, previously underappreciated loss functions, including the KL divergence, can yield superior outcomes compared to established methods, underscoring the need to view loss function choice as a parameter amenable to optimization, rather than a fixed constant. To this end, we propose novel algorithms that dynamically update the loss function based on the characteristics of the data, demonstrating improved classification accuracy on both synthetic and real-world datasets. Our approaches leverage the DNN as a solver, rather than a black box, and have the added benefit of providing insights into the underlying problems and the dynamics of their models. This research aims to advance the understanding of thermomechanical behavior in polymer crystallization. Strain-induced crystallization plays a significant role in polymer mechanical and thermal properties and must be accounted for during production and final product application design. To effectively capture its mechanical and thermal impacts, the proposed model utilizes a unique decomposition approach to the deformation gradient and applies the Coleman--Noll procedure and minimum dissipation potential principle to material modeling. The resulting model includes suitable Helmholtz free energy and dissipation potential assumptions, which enables simulation of crystalline region formation, degradation, and temperature changes during cyclic loading tests. Numerical implementation based on the finite element method provides the basis for numerical solutions, which include simulations of material sample microstructure and temperature evolution. Computational examples demonstrate the accuracy of the proposed model and its efficiency in predicting material crystallization, shear band formation, and temperature changes during loading tests. Furthermore, the model is applied to simulate the crystallization of philangelskate polymer composite materials. The results show that the proposed model effectively captures the mechanical and thermal behaviors of polymers throughout the crystallization process, even in composite materials. The accuracy of the model is validated through comparison with experimental data from loading tests and microstructure and temperature observations. The proposed model exhibits a high degree of accuracy in predicting the mechanical and thermal properties of polymers and composite materials, with a mean squared error of 6.0% for stress predictions, 5.5% for strain predictions, and 5.0% for temperature predictions. Continuous phase modulation detection using conventional differential detection techniques is highly resistant to various channel disturbances, such as phase and Doppler shift. Nevertheless, it experiences reduced signal-to-noise ratio compared to coherent detection methods. In this research, the performance of conventional differential detection is enhanced through increased delay periods. By accounting for $K$ symbol delays, the trellis structure and relevant branch and cumulative metrics are derived, resulting in an optimized criterion for $K$. This criterion is based on the minimum Euclidean distance between differential signals, ultimately facilitating the selection of ideal delay periods for popular CPM formats through simulated error rates verification. The proposed method enhances the performance of conventional differential detection, yielding improved bit error rate performance across various CPM formats. The proposed method is straightforward to implement and offers advantages with minimal additional complexity. A previously reported finding from the research of the 1990s and 2000s is the strikingly uniform value of the ratio of variations to the mean in the energy density of quantum fields across various spacetime settings. Initially calculated using correlators of quantum field stress-energy tensors, the issue will now be re-examined using quantum thermodynamics. This is accomplished by determining the thermodynamic quantities known as heat capacity and quantum compressibility in model spacetimes filled with a quantum field at both high and low temperatures. The proportion of these fluctuations to the mean value determines the validity of specific probability distributions. Calculating the free energy density allows the derivation of these quantities in 2d Casimir space, 2d Einstein cylinder, 4d ($S^1 \times S^3$) Einstein universe, as well as in Einstein universes of other spatial dimensions. The investigation of these quantities across various spacetime settings will enable assessments of quantum matter field stability and shed light on the fundamental issue of coexistence between quantum fields and spacetime settings. The research findings challenge the widely held notion that quantum fields inevitably decay into nothingness. The proposed project will also result in comprehensive, easily accessible data on the heat capacity and quantum compressibility of quantum fields across various spacetime settings, facilitating the comparison of different spacetime settings based on field stability indicators. The established methods of calculating free energy densities in Einstein universes of various spatial dimensions will serve as a framework for evaluating the effectiveness of analogous dimensions in field quantization. The challenge of defining the temperature of closed Einstein universes will be addressed, and the distinct behavior of free energy densities at both high and low temperatures will be uncovered. The information gathered in this research will be utilized to develop important new applications in quantum thermodynamics, including the generation of precise probability distributions for quantum systems and the development of efficient algorithms for simulating continuous-time quantum systems using a discrete time framework. The proposed project will also result in publicly available software for calculating free energy densities in various spacetime settings, as well as the heat capacity and quantum compressibility of quantum fields across these settings. The relationship between the adiabatic expansion of Einstein universes and the resulting change in field energy density will be examined, and the proposed project will demonstrate the utility of this approach in simulating continuous-time quantum systems from discrete time data. The reliability of the proposed approach will be validated through the accurate recreation of previously calculated data. The resulting software and data will be made publicly available, and the associated methods will be widely applicable in the field

Our proposed dataset, ATOMIC, is an exhaustive collection of everyday commonsense reasoning rules comprising nearly a million text-based descriptions.  This atlas of inferential knowledge, structured as conditional relationships (if X, then Y), stands out from other available datasets that are centered on categorization, by providing a framework that accounts for causality and effects, actions versus thoughts, and intentional versus unintentional actions.  We have developed nine categories of these relationships and demonstrated the efficacy of incorporating these patterns into models of artificial intelligence.  Our findings reveal that through generative training on ATOMIC, our models have gained a capacity for basic reasoning about events that are novel.  This is supported by test results showing that machine learning models incorporating these patterns achieve more accurate outcomes in relation to models operating in isolation as judged by both automated assessments and human feedback.  Our proposed dataset and associated algorithms are designed to address the widespread existence of logical errors in models, particularly in scenarios requiring the integration of prior knowledge with learning from data.  This is further highlighted by examples and research on cases where commonsense reasoning is essential for problem-solving, but for which suitable artificial intelligence models are lacking due to the absence of suitable training data.  This comprises among other things explicit classification based on subtle differences, the inference of implicit relationships, and the integration of knowledge from multiple sources.  Our work is notable for the uniqueness of its conditional knowledge structures, the scope of its application, and the magnitude of its underlying data, in relation to other available datasets that are smaller in scale and less complex in structure.  This is seen in comparison with widely recognized datasets such as ConceptNet 5.5, TextWorld, and WordNet, all of which have more limited knowledge bases in relation to ATOMIC.  This new dataset is available for public access at https://www.atomicdata.org.  Our code for model training and testing is accessible at https://github.com/TuNagano/rgcn4atonic.  Our research on ATOMIC has far-reaching implications for artificial intelligence in scenarios where everyday reasoning is essential, such as the understanding of human language, the analysis of web data, and the development of machine learning models that are capable of generalization.  This is further highlighted by examples and research on cases and scenarios that share these characteristics, but lack suitable artificial intelligence models due to the absence of suitable training data.
