In recent years, graph-based neural network methods, like graph neural networks, have effectively tackled classification and link prediction tasks by capturing complex data representations. However, most current applications rely on static graph models, which fail to account for the ever-changing connectivity structure observed in highly dynamic systems. Utilizing static models in such scenarios leads to subpar performance. In contrast, modeling temporal changes in graph structure offers a more comprehensive understanding, going beyond classification capabilities. Current approaches primarily focus on correlation-based representations, neglecting directed relationships, which are essential in numerous domains, particularly neuroscience. Our novel model, DECENNT, seeks to address this limitation by introducing a directed and dynamic graph, trained through neural network optimization, that reflects downstream classification and prediction tasks. DECENNT outperforms existing solutions in multiple tasks and provides task-specific dynamic graphs that are easily interpretable. When applied to neuroimaging data, DECENNT-generated graphs demonstrate high consistency with existing research and provide supplementary insights. Moreover, DECENNT's temporal attention mechanism identifies pivotal time periods for predictive downstream tasks from complex time series data. Our code is available at https://github.com/ghdeng/DECENNT.

Animals move through their environments for different purposes such as foraging, settling into a habitat, capturing prey, evading predators or mating. The vast array of biodiversity is linked to the diverse locomotory methods that different species employ, with many creatures using their legs, wings, fins, and other appendages to navigate their surroundings. This document refers to the movement of biological species as biolocomotion, presenting a computational method to automatically identify biolocomotion from raw video footage. A distinguishing feature of biolocomotion is its combination of forward movement and asymmetrical oscillatory motion, absent in the movement of non-living objects. By utilizing this trait along with differences between the overall movement of an object and the movement of its individual parts, a detection algorithm is created to determine whether the observed motion corresponds to a biological entity. Alternatively, a second approach based on a combination of common features and machine learning is presented for comparison purposes. This discovery has implications for various applications such as animal-plant interaction analysis, animal behavior study, and environmental monitoring. The advent of big data processing has created significant computational challenges when dealing with large-scale linear systems and matrix inversion, prompting the development of fast approximate iterative matrix inversion methods. Leveraging GPU acceleration, researchers have explored alternatives to classic direct inversion, leading to various methods such as Neumann Series, Newton iteration, and Successive Over-Relaxation. In response, we introduce a new iterative algorithm called 'Nested Neumann' (NN), which builds on the Neumann Series by incorporating a free iterative update of the preconditioning matrix, utilizing an inception depth to enhance convergence. Theoretical analysis has proven that NN meets three key conditions: it converges given the spectral norm condition is satisfied, achieves a convergence rate of one order higher for each additional inception depth, and has an optimal inception depth of one or two, subject to RAM constraints. Furthermore, we derive an explicit formula for the NN applicable to massive sparse matrices at an increased computational cost, demonstrating its analytic equivalence to higher-order iterations. The Nested Neumann method can be used for matrix inversion in positive semi-definite matrices and general linear systems, including sparse, non-sparse, and complex matrices. Empirical evaluation across multiple platforms reveals that NN outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods, including the widely-used Conjugate Gradient algorithm, by a two-order-of-magnitude in computation time, following a 4-order-of-magnitude shift in problem size. Nonetheless, we acknowledge that NN may experience difficulty with poor initialisation, requiring further research into innovative initiation strategies. The analysis includes massive top- and bottom-quark contributions at the NLO QCD level, with the top-quark contribution further detailed in the heavy top-quark effective theory, up to the N^3LO QCD and incorporating a soft expansion for the $\mathcal{CP}$-even light Higgs boson. The calculations for the $\mathcal{CP}$-odd component of the light Higgs boson and the heavy Higgs bosons are carried out up to the NNLO QCD level. The study also considers two-loop electroweak effects and SUSY QCD corrections at the NLO level, with corrections for squark effects dependent on the phases of the complex parameters demonstrated. The analysis highlights the importance of incorporating correct on-shell properties for the external Higgs bosons through finite wave function normalisation factors, obtained from the $\texttt{FeynHiggs}$ code. The results have been incorporated into an extension of the $\texttt{SusHi}$ code, referred to as $\texttt{SusHiMi}$. The dataset provides the basis for a range of studies, including an examination of residual theoretical uncertainties, a discussion of phase-dependent effects, and an exploration of phenomenological implications. The associated code has been designed to facilitate the incorporation of the predicted cross-sections into general purpose Monte Carlo codes via the $\texttt{SusHiMi}$ interface. The results highlighted here are the outcome of a collaborative project involving the MSSM working group. Contextual linear bandits is an important model with various applications and has seen a significant surge in interest lately. This surge particularly occurred in the realm of wireless applications, where communication constraints pose a significant performance obstacle. Especially in scenarios where context dimensions are substantial. This paper addresses a decentralized, memoryless contextual linear bandit learning problem. In this problem, agents that observe the context and make decisions are physically isolated from the learner. This learner executes the learning process but remains unaware of the context. Contexts are assumed to be generated randomly and a new approach is presented. This approach uses approximately five context dimensions' worth of information when the context distribution is unknown and uses zero bits when the distribution is known. This approach offers nearly the same regret bound as if contexts were fully observable. This achievement is notable as it outperforms existing bounds by a significant margin. This achievement particularly occurred when the time horizon is substantial. When the distribution is known the approach offers an information theoretically optimal bound. This approach is particularly effective in large scale wireless applications. Our study investigates outcomes of the Event Shape Engineering method implemented in lead-lead collisions at a 2.76 TeV collision energy.  Events with the same level of centrality but varied average flow are used to investigate initial state conditions.  Results reveal that the event-shape selection's influence on the elliptic flow coefficient is unaffected by transverse momentum.  Also found is that charged hadron distributions are steeper for events exhibiting higher-than-average elliptic flow, indicating interactions between radial and elliptic flow phenomena.  Consequences of the Event Shape Engineering method on charged hadron flows in polarized and deformed collisions are also explored, with derived expressions showing that the ratio of charged hadron flows in polarized and deformed collisions is directly proportional to the initial state's angular momentum density.  Ultimately, this research enhances the Event Shape Engineering method's capabilities and provides a theoretical framework for the ratio of charged hadron flows in polarized and deformed collisions.  Key results are also compared to SPHENIX collaboration data, with observed agreement between data and simulation results from the HYDRO+MUSIG model.  A key finding from this research is the presence of radial flow's influence on charged hadron distributions in nuclear collisions, leading to predictions for the ALICE collaboration's upcoming experiments.  Finally, this research paves the way for Event Shape Engineering applications in proton-nucleus and nucleus-nucleus collisions beyond lead-lead cases.  A software tool called Event Shape Engineering Explorer is also developed to facilitate intuitive exploration of data and predicted outcomes.  This research's findings and accompanying tools are made available for wide use within the particle physics community.  Key aspects of the paper are summarized in the paper's appendix.  Furthermore, this research's knowledge can be expanded upon using current and future experimental data, as well as advancements in theoretical models. Section 2 explains the Event Shape Engineering method and Altitude Angle distribution analysis, while Section 3 introduces the HYDRO+MUSIG model's simulations and the Event Shape Engineering Explorer tool.  Section 4 explores initial state conditions in polarized and deformed collisions, while Section 5 examines hadron distribution outcomes in event shape engineered events.  Section 6's research compares with SPHENIX and ALICE collaboration data, and provides predictions for future ALICE experiments.  Section 7 summarizes the paper's knowledge and outcomes. This work utilizes the concepts from Generalized Degrees of Freedom (GDoF) analyses and extremal network theory to examine the extremal gain resulting from optimal power control in contrast to binary (on/off) power control in large interference networks, focusing on uncovering new theoretical insights. Numerical studies have shown that in many real-world applications, binary power control is near optimal, however the extremal analysis indicates there are settings where the gain from optimal power control can be substantial, also offering bounds on extremal gain values from a GDoF perspective. As its primary contribution, this research precisely defines the extremal GDoF gain of optimal over binary power control as proportional to $\sqrt{K}$, where $\Theta\left(\sqrt{K}\right)$ represents the ratio, for any number $K$. It is worth noting that this gain can vary between the minimum $\lfloor \sqrt{K}\rfloor$ and a maximum of $2.5\sqrt{K}$, for any number of $K$. Further investigation into networks that reach the extremal gain reveal they could potentially be described as multi-tiered, heterogeneous networks. A note is made that due to its focus on long-term analysis, this gain characterizations hold value primarily in theoretical contexts rather than as contradictions to binary power control generally being near optimal in everyday, non-long-term scenarios. This research is a component of a larger study that also introduces new power control strategies and evaluates their performance. The resulting extremal theory was uncovered through a combination of both intuitive understanding and rigorous, mathematical analysis. The characterizations obtained from this extremal theory can be utilized in GDoF studies of various power control strategies and also provide a framework for understanding the extremities of itself. The study and its findings are demonstrated through an example of optimal power control in large interference networks with fixed user rates, also known as CLS-CMACC. The methodologies developed in this research are unique in that they are entirely separate from the conventional, statistical approaches used in general extremal theory. The distinction of this research also lies in the fact that the networks it studies are so large that they incorporate multiple, heterogeneous tiers. The study of these networks reveals a relationship between their gain and the number of users, a connection that the research calls the 'extremal gain of optimal power control'. The term 'extremal' is chosen because the research finds that the majority of networks, even those that are quite complex, do not reach the extremal gain. This study introduces an advanced integration method for simulating multiple steps of particle collisions in flows. Due to the need for smaller time steps for resolving particle collisions, traditional models can become computationally expensive for large-scale simulations involving numerous particles. Existing methods often involve artificially lengthening collision time steps to several times the time steps used in flow simulations, however this can lead to biased simulation results. Our multiple-time-step integration algorithm utilizes distinct time steps for fluid flow, fluid-particle interactions, and particle collisions. We successfully tested this method for particle collisions and demonstrated improved accuracy by matching simulation results with experimental data obtained using traditional models. Our algorithm was then integrated into a simulation of complex sediment transport with thousands of particles, comparing it to the standard method that artificially lengthens collision time steps. Our results showed that artificially stretching collision time steps leads to particles being too flexible and affects the turbulence and distribution of particles, whereas our algorithm reduces computational cost to one tenth of the standard method while retaining nearly identical accuracy. Our simulation of particle collisions was further validated using high-speed imaging, showing that our algorithm accurately models collision outcomes and shapes compared to experimental data. Our algorithm has the potential to be applied to the simulation of various multiple-body interactions in fluids with solid objects. Our code is available at https://github.com/ghaman/DTDTN for public use. Overall, our algorithm provides a reliable and efficient solution for simulating complex interactions between numerous particles in fluids. Our simulation of sediment transport with particles was further validated using a flume experiment, showing that our algorithm accurately models particle enlargement, turbulence, and distribution. A significant issue in legged locomotion research is the uncertainty that arises when robots navigate deformable terrain. This challenge stems from the unpredictable behavior of terrain dynamics caused by ground deformation. Developing efficient and stable control systems for robots moving on soft ground poses an even greater problem. This project focuses on controlling a one-legged hopping robot to jump to a predetermined height. Initially, a simulated environment representing a soft ground was created using a discrete element method (DEM) based on spherical granular material. This simulation was utilized to derive models of ground reaction forces through the resistive force theory (RFT). A feedforward force control system was developed and tested in conjunction with the DEM simulation. To account for discrepancies in the RFT model's predictions of ground reaction forces, a feedback control system was employed. As a result, the robot successfully tracked its intended trajectory, reached the desired height in five hops, and reduced height errors compared to a feedforward control system alone. Furthermore, by increasing the robot's foot area from 1cm^2 to 49cm^2, the feedback controller demonstrated its ability to adapt to changing ground reaction forces, even when the foot size was comparable to the diameter of individual grains. Ultimately, the robot was able to reach a height of 24cm, only 0.4cm shorter than predicted, despite experiencing significant ground deformation during each hop. This research showcases a control system that effectively manages the uncertain forces encountered on soft ground by adjusting the applied forces to achieve the desired movement. This approach has the potential to be scalable to robot scenarios involving multiple legs on deformable terrain. This approach also offers a promising framework for controlling robots that navigate dynamic, complex environments subject to significant alterations over time. This approach has been tested in a comprehensive simulation of a one-legged robot hopping on a solid floor made up of thousands of individually modeled grains of sand. This simulation models real-world conditions seen in actual robot experiments. This approach has been compared to existing control systems and has been found to provide more accurate results even in the presence of substantial noise. This research paves the way for extending this control approach to robots with multiple legs that navigate dynamic, complex environments with a wide range of granular materials. In this paper, the contact interaction model is applied to the study of meson elastic form factors. Quark and meson dressed masses are derived from gap and Bethe-Salpeter equations, with a specific focus on mesons comprised of distinct flavor quarks. An analysis of the generic $M\gamma \to M$ scattering process is performed. Furthermore, calculations for the charge radii of various meson types, including scalars, pseudoscalars, vectors, and axial-vectors, yield explicit elastic form factor values. The proposed model's formulation allows for predictions on the phenomena of glue radiation and anomalous chromoelectric momenta within mesons. The research presents explicit equations for form factors in terms of the 6-fold Borel integral, allowing for an examination of the stability of these integrals under variations of the parameters involved. Nonetheless, for many meson types, particularly those with larger masses, form factor equations prove too complex to solve through the 6-fold Borel method used here. A study on the phenomena of glue radiation within mesons also yields predictions on distinct flavor quark combinations' bound state masses. Ultimately, this research provides a comprehensive foundation for extending the study of elastic form factors to include additional ingredients of QCD, such as pseudo-scalar meson glue radiation and anomalous chromoelectric momenta. The developed framework is versatile and has the potential to be applied to a broad range of quark and meson combinations. The paper is self-contained, with detailed appendices available for the benefit of readers already familiar with the subject. The research under consideration is a part of a broader study conducted by the author, with related works listed in the references below. A related study conducted by the author is also mentioned in the text, where the approach of contact interaction model was applied to quark quark annihilations into lepton pairs, which influenced the present analysis. The knowledge gained from this experience proved invaluable in achieving a deeper understanding of the approach. A notable aspect of this paper is the explicit derivation of the Borel transformed Bethe-Salpeter amplitude equations, which are crucial for determining the elastic form factors of mesons. Although the approach of contact interaction model provides a suitable description of various quark and meson combinations' properties, the research reveals that the Borel transformed Bethe-Salpeter amplitude equations exhibit a level of complexity that challenges solution through the 6-fold Borel method used here. Organizational frameworks like information hierarchies are commonly used to present complex data and simplify navigation, yet the automatic generation methods available today don't account for the interconnections in modern information networks. Presently, most techniques represent topics as abstract probabilities rather than tangible components of the underlying network, and many lack the scalability needed for web-based applications. In contrast, we propose a novel approach, Hierarchical Document Topic Model (HDTM), utilizing a non-parametric distributed processing model that effectively extracts meaningful hierarchies from large networks, even at a massive data scale, as evidenced by our experiments using three smaller datasets and Wikipedia's full content. The results show that our approach matches the accuracy of state-of-the-art methods while offering substantial time and memory efficiency gains, making it an attractive solution for scaling topic hierarchies to extremely large datasets. The code used in our research is now publicly accessible via GitHub, and we have additionally conducted studies on generating hierarchies from existing models, sorting topics by their hierarchical depth, and integrating the approach with both supervised and unsupervised learning methods. The findings and the associated code provide a foundation for future research and applications based on the proposed model. The HDTM approach has utility in a wide range of applications, including but not limited to, the optimization of search engine results, the enhancement of text summarization, and the improvement of personalized product recommendations based on product category hierarchies. The explicit representation of topics as hierarchical structures also offers future research possibilities into the visualization of topics, the detection of community structures within networks, and the integration of external metadata into the model. The underlying model's flexibility allows for the incorporation of additional information, enabling the detection of complex patterns in large-scale networks and the creation of applications tailored to specific domains. The code and the associated knowledge graphs are publicly accessible at https://github.com/yinzhq/hdtm. The developed code includes an initial exploration of sorting topics by their hierarchical depth, as well as an introduction to the underlying Mallet API, which is now deprecated, and the recommended replacement CMU's own Stanford-Algorithms package, specifically the HierarchicalTopicModel class. Quantum annealing and quenching exhibit opposite characteristics in their temporal development within a quantum system: quantum annealing delves into the equilibrium phases of a Hamiltonian through gradual parameter modifications and serves as a problem-solving technique for intricate optimization problems, whereas quenching involves sudden, abrupt changes to the Hamiltonian resulting in non-equilibrium scenarios. This study investigates the interconnection between the two scenarios and reveals that the minimal point of the annealing gap, a critical obstacle in quantum annealing algorithms, can be determined from a dynamical quench parameter that defines the quantum state following the quench. When combined with statistical tools, such as neural network training, this relationship between quench and annealing dynamics can be utilized to accurately reproduce the annealing gap's functional behavior based solely on the quench data. As such, partial or full understanding of the annealing gap, obtained in this manner, can be employed to devise optimized quantum annealing protocols, leading to a tangible improvement in solution-finding efficiency. These findings stem from simulations of random Ising Hamiltonians that model complex, intractable instances of the exact cover problem. As such, they demonstrate the practical applicability of quench-driven learning for quantum annealing. This approach's effectiveness is measured through comparison with quantum annealing alone and other quench-related approaches, revealing a consistent improvement of approximately an order of magnitude in terms of the optimal annealing time when learning from the quench data. This occurs alongside a comparable increase when the input Hamiltonian's annealing time is increased from $20\mu s$ to $200\mu s$ when implementing the random Ising Hamiltonian simulation. Ultimately, this research highlights the quench-annealing connection's potential to enhance quantum annealing algorithms that rely on learning from the quench-generated quantum state, offering a promising, experimentally-feasible strategy for improving the efficiency of quantum annealing. This efficiency-enhancing approach can be readily applied to various optimization problems and algorithms used within quantum annealing, as evidenced by successful simulation transfer across distinct problem instances and algorithms following the same quench-annealing dynamics. This transfer achieves an increase of three orders of magnitude in the optimal annealing time when transitioning from quantum annealing alone to the combined approach, while maintaining the exact same success rate in solution-finding. This success is measured through comparison with quantum annealing alone and other quench-related approaches in complex problem instances comprising both random graph and Ising Hamiltonians following the same quench-annealing dynamics. extent to which it can be reduced to a simplified one-band Hubbard model. 
Screening of the $s$-like orbital's influence is a critical factor here. 
Without screening, an isolated highly-correlated band yields an
antiferromagnetic ground state. For mild screening, strong correlations cause
the more freely moving $s$-electrons to shift to the $d$-band and the nickelate
then becomes a half-filled, highly insulating state. This case is notably
distinct from high-$T_c$ cuprates, with $s$-wave symmetry being a more
expected phenomenon. 
On the other hand, strong screening leads to a mixture of filled and weakly
coupled $s$ and $d_{x^2-y^2}$ bands and results in self-doped $d$ orbital and
$d$-wave pairing tendencies emerging. 
Interestingly, strong screening allows for another one-band physics approximation,
this time incorporating significant weight transfer when an extra filled $s$-band
is included, exhibiting both one-band physics and Kondo-lattice-like behavior,
which arises solely from this single model. 
Thus, the essential physics of nickelates can be captured using a one-band
model, yet the underlying physics is intricately tied to the specific band
screening it experiences, making the nickelate family particularly complex and
intriguing.

As a compact star's density increases, sound velocity approaches the conformal limit at high densities, satisfying the causality limit while its detailed behavior remains disputed. It's hypothesized that dense matter sound velocity can be an indicator of a deconfinement phase transition, possibly exhibiting a distinctive relationship with density. Our work delves into the fundamental properties of dense matter sound velocity and the adiabatic index within neutron stars, quark stars, and hybrid stars. Consequently, this could result in a denser star with similar mass, thus providing the groundwork for a new type of quark star equation of states that may be tested through high-precision pulsar radius measurements. We investigate a variety of non-classical states made up of superposed, both squeezed and displaced number states, examining their phase space structure in relation to Heisenberg limited sensitivity in parameter estimation. Certain combinations of squeezing and displacement are identified that maintain over 99% state fidelity compared to a highly sensitive reference state, known as a compass state, which also exhibits equivalent variance in small shifts measurements. Both proposed and compass states display analogous behavior as average photon number changes. Notably, in practical applications, the compass state's minimal number variance when coherent amplitude is low may indicate its suitability for estimating damping parameters. Additionally, both states exhibit analogous number distribution patterns, suggesting they could be used to estimate similar parameters with equivalent precision. Despite sharing the same number distribution pattern, the compass state exhibits distinct behavior in quadrature amplitude oscillations between measurements, suggesting distinct sensitivity to certain parameters. Despite displaying equivalent variance in certain measurements, the compass state exhibits higher amplitude in another measurement setting. Consequently, the impact of using the compass state instead of proposed states would depend on specific conditions and requirements. Ultimately, both states demonstrate the efficacy of using squeezed and displaced number states for achieving Heisenberg limited sensitivity in parameter estimation. Furthermore, both states meet the requirements for achieving optimal damping resistance in Markovian environments. Given their distinct characteristics, both states may be used in different scenarios, offering a foundation for developing novel protocols that combine efficient damping resistance with Heisenberg limited sensitivity. Experimentally creating these states using a combined beam splitter and parametric amplifier setup is also demonstrated. Both states have been successfully generated with achievable experimental parameters, with average photon number varying from 1 to 20, and coherent amplitude amplitude varying from 0 to 5, providing a practical foundation for implementing them in various applications. The simulation models are available for public use on GitHub at the following link: https://github.com/Yue-Alice/SqueezedDisplacedNumberStates. The Heisenberg limited sensitivity in parameter estimation can be achieved using specific non-classical states of light, enabling over fond performance in various applications, including ultra-precise measurement of tiny shifts, damping parameters in practical scenarios, and wavefunction tomography. Among non-classical states, squeezed and displaced number states offer Heisenberg limited sensitivity while requiring lower average photon number compared to compass states, which have the advantage of minimal variance in coherent amplitude, but may be more challenging to generate using available technology, with a proposed combined beam splitter and parametric amplifier setup that is both practical and realistic. A phenomenon called vertical shear instability (VSI) is observed in protoplanetary disk systems requiring quick cooling of gases, potentially influencing how particles develop and settle within these areas. While the VSI can generate turbulence and, as a result, impact the development and settling of particles, dust depletion might also suppress the VSI, as it limits gas cooling efficiency. In a research effort, we examine the potential stabilizing effects that particle growth has on VSI, focusing on a theoretical analysis and a created model that takes into account particle size development and settling behavior. Combining this model with stability calculations, we mapped areas in protoplanetary disks susceptible to VSI, analyzing its peak growth rates in various locations. As particles develop and settle around the midplane of these systems, VSI's reach diminishes due to decreased shear velocity. In a default model with a 0.01 solar mass disk, an enhancement from 10-micron to 1 millimeter particles reduces the VSI's growth rate by over ten times. As dust development restricts VSI-driven turbulence, it may encourage further dust growth, contributing to particle settlement seen in certain disks, including the HL Tau disk system. In addition, the minimal impact of VSI in mature disks, like TT Aus, might be attributed to extensive dust development. In a model with a 0.1 solar mass disk, VSI's reach is largely limited to the inner regions, where temperature conditions support significant gas cooling, further supporting the theory that dust development significantly influences VSI's effects by limiting gas cooling, rather than altering particle dynamics directly. In the HL Tau disk case, the reduction of VSI in inner regions is more pronounced due to the presence of a disk wind. In a further analysis, a correlation is observed between the visitability of VSI in inner regions and disk masses (M), with a power of 1.86, indicating that the stability of these areas depends on mass more than other factors. In a prognostic model, we predict the visitability of VSI in inner regions based on a mass and a timescale, which could influence future observations, presenting a possible explanation for the decrease in VSI in the HL Tau disk system. In a final consideration, the interaction between the VSI and the GIA (Giant Planet Migration-induced Instability) in protoplanetary disks remains a subject of research that is worthy of further exploration. If the VSI is indeed suppressed by the GIA, it could, in turn, hinder massive planet formation

This research focuses on harmonic functions within the context of a particular type of manifold where the Ricci curvature decreases over time and the scalar curvature remains constant. We have derived a key theorem demonstrating that bounded harmonic functions are constant in this specific type of manifold, without relying on an established growth estimate. Consequently, this result implies that the set of all harmonic functions that grow at a polynomial rate on these manifolds is finite-dimensional. Our proof involves an innovative approach, as we have substituted an ancient solution with a related solution that has a more limited scope, and then established its equivalence to a solution with specific properties, on which the existing Liouville theorem can be applied. Additionally, we have an alternative proof utilizing an estimate of growth based on Harman's approach. However, researchers have recently discovered methods like Neural Cleanse and ABS to be vulnerable to triggers that are dynamic, meaning they are unaffected by pattern or location, thus compromising their reliability. Moreover, the research revealed that learning from large, clean datasets like Wikipedia text or common image datasets like MNIST, does not prevent the network from being susceptible to these elusive backdoors, thus posing a significant risk to real-world applications of machine learning. For the most straightforward species, including oxygen-based molecules such as water, carbon dioxide, carbon monoxide, and hydroxyl, there are significant gaps in spectral reference data in some frequency ranges. This study gathers existing spectral information about these cations to pinpoint areas where additional research is necessary to enhance the comprehension of cometary evolution. In the context of a Parameter Server, learning a model from distributed data on a graph is a challenging task, especially when it comes to Federated Learning. A significant obstacle in this process is the substantial communication required between nodes and the server. A common strategy used to address this issue involves each node making several local model updates before sharing the updated model with the server. Although this method reduces communication costs, it introduces statistical disparities among the nodes' data sets, leading to slower model convergence and biases. This paper explores the application of random walk learning algorithms to tackle these issues by exploiting existing connections between nodes, as they typically require less communication with the server. A random walk is proposed where a node shares the updated model with a neighbor, with the aim of visiting more informative nodes more frequently. This goal is framed as a sleeping multi-armed bandit problem to devise an efficient node sampling strategy that generates variance-reduced gradient estimates. A novel adaptive random walk learning algorithm is introduced and proven to converge theoretically. Moreover, our results demonstrate its superior performance compared to other random walk algorithms. Additionally, guidelines are provided for practicing researchers on implementing this algorithm, including data preprocessing and hyperparameter selection. A sample code is available on a public repository for reference. Experimentally, our algorithm is shown to perform better than other random walk algorithms, even with heterogenous data sets, and it is considered a scalable and efficient solution for large-scale Federated Learning tasks. A future direction explored in this research could involve combining the learner with the server that generates the model, along with evaluating the algorithm on real-world datasets. To facilitate online predictions, we developed a new sparse approximation technique with enhanced performance compared to current rejection-based methods. With policy-dependent value function representations, our approach ensures that the value function's posterior reflects the underlying policy, ensuring offline policy evaluation efficacy.  In contrast, policy-independent representations, such as TD-zero, may not provide an accurate value function basis for offline policy evaluation.  Consequently, our approach is most effective when combined with policy-dependent algorithms like SARSA.  On the other hand, our SPGP-TD variant, which maintains a model of the environment, appears to be a more general approach that can be applied to policy-independent algorithms like TD-zero, but requires more samples to obtain a reliable value function basis.  Ultimately, our research demonstrates the feasibility and advantages of using Gaussian Process-based TD learning for offline policy evaluation in underwater robot navigation. By direct resolution and reconstruction, new exact solutions for this two-fluid case are found. Additionally, three theorems applicable to the single-fluid scenario can be adapted to yield two-fluid solutions from their single-fluid counterparts. These theorems include the \(f\)-form theorem, the Harko theorem, and the \(f\)-constant theorem, all of which generate specific cases. These solutions and theorems can serve as benchmarks for other numerical and analytical methods used to solve the two-fluid Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff equations. The solutions obtained satisfy the boundedness condition for the radial component of the Riemann tensor and comply with the causality constraint imposed by the speed of light. The case of an isotropic fluid reduces to known results, demonstrating the method's versatility. The obtained solutions have been applied to construct models of compact stars, including neutron star masses and radius-range plots. The proposed method offers a novel, generally covariant, and anisotropic approach to solving the two-fluid Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff equations, facilitating the creation of realistic models of compact stars comprising superdense nuclear matter and bulk dark matter. The resulting equations and solutions can be used to study relativistic stars made of two fluids with distinct properties across a broad range of densities. The achieved solutions have been applied to model neutron stars with a solid crust, partially or entirely, and the obtained results demonstrate the method's capability to describe multiple-star configurations. Most current sequence-to-sequence based Grammatical Error Correction methods focus primarily on generating more pseudo data to improve performance. In contrast, little work addresses the challenge of adapting GEC to new domains with limited resources. This paper treats various GEC domains as separate tasks and proposes a novel approach, grounded in meta-learning, that achieves few-shot domain adaptation without relying on pseudo data. Leveraging rich source domains, we establish a starting point for our model's parameters that facilitates efficient adaptation on scarce resource target domains. The proposed method is applied to adapting GEC models for the native languages of second language learners. To validate our approach, we utilized nine languages as source domains and five languages as target domains in the L1 GEC domain adaptation dataset, with results showing that it outperforms the baseline multi-task transfer learning approach by a 0.50 F score on average and enables successful adaptation to new target domains with as little as 200 parallel sentences. Moreover, our approach succeeds in GEC tasks with different levels of formality, such as adapting the GEC model for the writing styles found in web forums and research papers. All models and code are available for public use at https://github.com/SuqinTian/MetaGJT.

The task of allocating non-divisible goods to self-interested agents, where the valuation functions add up, and without the possibility of making monetary transactions, presents an interesting problem in fair allocation. In our investigation, we focus on whether mechanisms exist that, regardless of the situation, produce equilibria that are fair allocations for the involved agents, using only their declared, rather than true values, as input. Specifically, we are examining whether mechanisms exist for two relaxations of envy-free allocation - namely, allocating one good (EF1) or any good (EFX) fairly. Through our exploration, we investigated two established methods for achieving these relaxed envy-free allocations in a non-selfish setting: Round-Robin, known for generating allocations that are fair up to one good for any number of agents, and a cut-and-choose method of Plaut and Roughgarden, known for generating allocations that are fair up to any good for two agents. In our investigation of Round-Robin, we discovered that all equilibria resulting from it are fair allocations that are up to one good with respect to their underlying values, whereas for the Plaut and Roughgarden method, we discovered that the corresponding allocations are fair up to any good, as well as satisfying a maximin share fairness condition. Moreover, we established that for any mechanism with two agents that always has pure Nash equilibria inducing EFX allocations, this latter fairness condition holds in a weakened form. Finally, we outlined the challenges and possible approaches to investigating the relationship between pure Nash equilibria and fair allocations that are up to any good in a self-interested setting involving two agents. In the process, we established a necessary and sufficient condition for a mechanism with two agents to have pure Nash equilibria inducing allocations that are fair up to any good. This condition, which we termed "strong convexity", can be considered as its own standalone contribution. It remains unclear whether mechanisms exist that, regardless of the situation, produce equilibria that are fair allocations for the involved agents, using only their declared, rather than true values, as input, for a number of agents greater than two. It is, however, possible to achieve this for a number of agents equal to any power of two. We also explored the relationship between pure Nash equilibria and fair allocations that are up to any good in a self-interested setting involving any number of agents, which is challenging due to the complexity of mapping pure Nash equilibria to relevant allocations fairly. UGC 8839, an exceptionally faint spiral galaxy, is characterized by minimal star formation except in a substantial HII region located in the extreme outer rim of its disk. A comparative study with four similar spiral galaxies reveals that the unusual star formation in UGC 8839 is likely attributed to a highly stable, dark matter-dominated disk. Despite being rare, the HII region in UGC 8839 isn't exceptional when considering the distribution of its luminosity, suggesting it's a natural feature of the galaxy. However, unlike the HII regions in the other galaxies studied, those in UGC 8839 exhibit a notable preference for more distant galactocentric radii. The unique dynamics of UGC 8839 provide new insights into the relationship between baryonic matter, dark matter, and the stability of galaxy disks, potentially linked to a rare, three-body gravitational interaction similar to that hypothesized for the Malin 1 system. This research is also relevant to the study of low-luminosity galaxies with active black holes at their centers, like NGC 4468, and offers a framework for comparing these galaxies to UGC 8839. A comparative analysis of the four galaxies with unusual outer star formation reveals that they all possess slow rotation rates and are likely the result of a specific rare galaxy interaction that occurs for only a short period. Therefore, these galaxies present themselves as a distinct class, named ulld galaxies. This study is also an early step towards understanding the development and ultimate fate of ulld galaxies. This research is published in the journal Monthly Notices of the Royal Astronomical Society. Using lattice QCD, a thorough investigation of correlation functions of two quark currents within a pion is conducted, yielding clear signals for nearly all significant combinations of quark field contractions except one. The results are further examined to determine how they vary with the mass of quarks and whether correlations between the quark and the corresponding antiquark play a significant role in the pion's properties. Our lattice findings are compared with theoretical predictions made through the application of chiral perturbation theory. Although these predictions generally align with our lattice-based results, some discrepancies are observed, particularly with regard to the dependence on the quark mass and the impact of quark-antiquark correlations. In addition, our lattice data support previous findings suggesting that the quark-complement channel does not contribute substantially to the two-quark current correlation functions of the pion. Our research highlights the importance of accurately defining the quark fields when studying two-quark current correlations within hadrons, particularly when using nearly exact methods to study QCD. It is also demonstrated that at lower quark masses, the dependence of these correlations on the quark mass is more pronounced than predicted by chiral perturbation theory. This discrepancy is more evident when considering the quark mass within the $\overline{m}_2/\overline{m}_1$ ratio, where the quark masses $\overline{m}_1$ and $\overline{m}_2$ are obtained from simulations conducted at different lattice spacing values. This phenomenon suggests that the bare quark mass may play a more intricate role in hadron physics than currently understood, potentially indicating that higher-order chiral perturbation theory is required to accurately describe the dependence on the quark mass. This research also paves the way for exploring similar correlations in other mesons and baryons, as well as in lattice studies of quantitative properties of hadron interactions. Our lattice codes used in this study have been made public on GitHub. Evaluating protoplanetary disk evolution is closely tied to understanding how
mass accretion rates are influenced by a star and its disk properties.
However, accurately using observed relations in this context is hampered by
not properly accounting for variations in mass accretion rates, a problem
especially prevalent in earlier stages of star formation. Conversely, we found
large-scale fluctuations in mass accretion rates of one specific object, XX
Cha, and how these results could affect our current understanding of T Tauri
stars. Comparing our current analysis with previous measurements from the
X-Shooter, we observed a mass accretion variability of approximately 2 dex in
XX Cha over the 11-year period from 2010 to 2021, a value considered
particularly large among T Tauri stars. If this degree of variability holds
for other T Tauri stars on similar or different timeframes, then its effect
on the constraints of disk evolution models could be more pronounced than we
once anticipated, and it also highlights a potential shortcoming of earlier
research on mass accretion variability that relied solely on the study of
spectral lines, and thus, may have significantly underestimated variability
for certain objects. Furthermore, the large variability observed in XX Cha
raises important questions about the validity of using mass accretion rates
derived from line strengths for long-term applications, and it also suggests
that a more comprehensive examination is necessary to ensure an accurate
comprehension of the mass accretion process, especially in the earlier
stages of star formation. Additionally, our analysis of XX Cha reveals a
significant decrease in mass accretion variability over time, and we propose
a possible explanation for this behavior tied to the star's and disk's
evolutionary stage. Ultimately, our research underlines the significance of
considering variability when interpreting observed relations of T Tauri stars,
and it also emphasizes the value of repeated measurements through spectral
analysis for a more precise and in-depth understanding of protoplanetary
disks. The detailed examination of this unique object also provides a
hypothetical picture of disk evolution for a T Tauri star exhibiting extreme
mass accretion variability. The research presented in this paper is based on

Offline learning for multiple interacting agents is crucial for developing
practical applications involving multiple interacting entities. Yet, offline learning often encounters issues due to differing levels of effectiveness among the agents' learned behavior. For example, if one agent has a random policy while the others are more skilled, existing offline methods can result in the team's performance suffering. To tackle this problem, we present a novel offline learning framework called Shared Individual Trajectories (SIT) that explicitly considers the diversity of individual trajectories. The SIT framework leverages an attention-based mechanism and a graph attention network (GAT) to prioritize high-quality experiences and encourage sharing of effective trajectories among the agents. Through rigorous evaluation, our approach achieves superior results on complex datasets, especially in scenarios with significant variations in data quality. Moreover, the theoretical foundation of our framework is underpinned by a formal expression of optimal offline learning, which provides insights into desirable individual trajectories and a comparison with existing approaches. To facilitate further research, we are releasing the SIT framework and associated resources publicly. In 1927, Einstein used the Solvay conference to pose a thought-provoking experiment that aimed to highlight the incompleteness of quantum mechanics. He utilized the instantaneous non-local phenomenon resulting from the collapse of a particle's wave function during measurement, famously described as'spooky action at a distance.' Prior to the influential Einstein-Podolsk-Rosen criticism of quantum mechanics' incompleteness, Einstein had already raised these concerns. We utilize the Stern-Gerlach experiment to illustrate how the instantaneous non-locality of the wave function's collapse and single-particle entanglement can give rise to the phenomenon of steering, enabling a party to influence another's quantum state based on measurement decisions made by the first party. In this process, the spreading of the entangled wave function is exploited over vast distances, demonstrating how the non-locality of single-particle entanglement allows the particle to discern the detector used by the influencing party. Consequently, despite counterarguments, our proof confirms that single-particle entanglement results in genuine non-local effects between distant locations, paving the way for its utilization in implementing truly non-local tasks. Additionally, our study highlights the distinction between genuine non-locality arising from single-particle entanglement and that stemming from two-particle entanglement. Moreover, it is demonstrated that single-particle entanglation with a vast range can be maintained over extensive distances between a local particle and a non-local, freely propagating entangled partner, thereby offering an alternative to two-particle entanglement in the implementation of non-locality-based quantum tasks and applications. Finally, the investigation emphasizes the significance of distinguishing between different types of non-locality in quantum mechanics, especially in experiments involving single-particle entanglation with extensive ranges. V392 Persei, classified as a dwarf nova that underwent a classic nova explosion in 2018, is an extraordinary object whose extreme evolution over nearly three years has been closely observed.  V392 Persei, which rapidly shrank from 2 days, exhibited early spectral characteristics pointing towards several massive ejections interacting and causing both gamma-ray and optical illumination through shock waves.  V392 Persei entered its Sun-constrained phase soon after its eruption but upon exiting it entered its nebular stage with evidence of the super-soft X-ray stage's lingering tail.  Post eruption spectra showed both a persistent narrow-line spectrum of the accretion disk as well as the fading of the ejected particles, which were illuminated by an intense ongoing X-ray emission.  Optical data reveal an orbital period of nearly three and a half days while the absence of the white dwarf spin frequency presents further evidence for a massive WD.  The pre and post nova energy distributions also indicate a massive accretion rate.  V392 Persei, unlike many novae and dwarf novae systems, did not switch to its initial low mass transfer configuration, but instead stayed in its high mass transfer state, which we believe is as a result of the irradiation of the companion by the massive nova explosion, thus it exhibits a level of similarity with another renowned system known as GK Persei.  The system is also observing a massive dust lane, which is a first among novae, and is observing a level of polarization that is uncommon, which could be as a result of the massive amount of dust present or possibly microlensing caused by the particular close orbit of the system.  If the latter is the case, which we believe it is, then this could serve as a first observational evidence of a WD of such a close orbit causing lensing effects on a massive companion it's interacting with.  V392 Persei's unique path suggests that it will switch to its initial configuration eventually, but for now, it remains an extraordinary object that deserves close monitoring, with many firsts observed that could serve as a reference for other similar systems in the future.  The extensive coverage it has seen has also allowed for the creation of multiple long-term predictions, including the expected decline in brightness, the possible outcomes of any possible further eruptions, as well as the likely outcomes of the two interacting masses continuing their present course.  The research the team conducted also revealed several discrepancies in previously published data, which they strive to rectify with the aim of providing a comprehensive understanding of this extraordinary object

A proposed precoder codebook and feedback encoding approach leverages Gaussian mixture models (GMMs) to construct codebooks and reduce information exchange between base station and mobile terminal. Initially, the base station trains a GMM using uplink signal samples, then creates a codebook based on GMM components, assigning one entry per component. Only the GMM is transferred to the mobile terminal, allowing it to find the most relevant codebook entry by measuring the responsibility of each GMM component to the received signal, without needing channel estimation. Feedback is transmitted as the index of the most responsible component and corresponding codebook entry, leading to enhanced performance over traditional approaches, notably in scenarios with limited pilot data transmission. Simulation results demonstrate the system's ability to adapt to changing environments, with the GMM approach showing higher eigenbeamforming gains than traditional codebooks, showcasing the system's potential for use in applications with frequent environmental changes, like vehicular networks. Codebook entry selection criteria and some common scenarios, such as motion-related GMM changes, are also examined. The system's source code is provided as supplemental material. The research focuses on a specific configuration, but codebook design and feedback encoding methods are generally applicable to various 5G scenarios. Overall, the study shows that GMM-based codebooks and feedback encoding can significantly improve the performance, reliability, and efficiency of communication systems. The approach has additional advantages, including reducing storage requirements for codebooks. The research underlying this study was previously published in WCNC 2022, with some updates presented here. A type of genuine two-dimensional crosscurrent that flows counter to the heat flux direction has been lacking in scientific knowledge since its one-dimensional counterpart was discovered. A setup for realizing these currents on a three-dimensional cubic lattice has been devised by coupling a Hofstadter model to two separate heat baths of varying temperatures. Research demonstrates that the robustness of these currents can withstand various imperfections and tilting within certain nonequilibrium conditions. Additionally, boundary currents with robust stability were found, and the condition of being three-dimensionally robust indicates they require tunneling capabilities across all three spatial dimensions. The model exhibits robust surface currents applicable to both bosons and fermions, and the mechanisms of discrete symmetries were found to significantly contribute to the surface currents' stability. The stability of these surface currents can be significantly enhanced by applying a three-dimensional robust coupling across multiple spatial dimensions, and the capability to withstand disorder, periodic potential changes, and temperature differences was demonstrated. The model also exhibits an exotic anyon phase that aligns with theoretical predictions made in 2013. The novel anyon phase that emerges in the coupled Hofstadter model exhibits an unusual anyon spectrum that has been elusive in scientific knowledge and can only be achieved when the system is placed in a truly two-dimensional crosscurrent condition. The anyon spectrum's uniqueness is characterized by a specific fraction, 6/5, which is unlike any known fraction including those associated with both the fractional quantum Hall effect and semions. The robust surface anyon phase that emerges in the coupled Hofstadter model shares some key characteristics with the anyon phase predicted for topological superconductivity, but the coupled Hofstadter model achieves this milestone without the need for any kind of coupling that involves spin. As a result, the anyon phase that emerges in the coupled Hofstadter model is considered non-Abelian, localized only on the surface, and is capable of withstanding various kinds of perturbations. We examine the formation of Population III binary remnants within nuclear star clusters using a semi-analytical model for the early universe. Our framework accounts for the movement of Population III binary remnants during the formation of the universe's structure and identifies which of these remnants fall into nuclear star clusters through gravitational interaction with field stars. Following this, we track their subsequent development within these clusters through gravitational encounters and gravitational waves, and predict the likelihood of mergers of Population III binary remnants. Our study shows that about 7.5% of Population III binary remnants become situated in the centres of galaxies and 5-50% of these will merge in nuclear star clusters at high redshifts. These events peak at z=5-7 with a merger rate of 0.4-10 years^-1 Gpc^-3. Our predictions also reveal that the most massive of these remnants primarily reside in small, low-mass nuclear star clusters formed in the early universe. These clusters host black holes of masses 40-85 M_\\odot that can produce detections similar to GW190521, specifically in a mass range typically found for pulsational pair-instability supernovae with a merger rate of 0.01-0.09 years^-1 Gpc^-3. Our model predicts observations of GW190521-like events, with a minimum mass of 57 M_\\odot for pulsational pair-instability supernovae, and suggests that a significant portion of the L-T relation is explained by Population III binary remnants in the centres of galaxies. Our study proposes that the most detailed GW detections will originate from the most massive of these remnants found in the most secluded, nuclear star clusters. Our model predicts a maximum mass of 85 M_\\odot for stable neutron stars formed from Population III progenitors, in agreement with theoretical predictions based on angular momentum. Our study provides a possible explanation for GW190521 along with its possible counterpart, SGR 1900+09, which could have originated from a merger of a neutron star and a quark star or black hole of a mass 40-85 M_\\odot formed from a pair-instability supernova. Our model also predicts a population of quark stars or black holes with masses 40-85 M_\\odot in the centres of galaxies. These could give rise to heavy binary mergers with known GW events, such as GW190814, with possible counterparts like 3E and Westerbork Imaging Array 1, which could have originated from mergers

In this study, we examine the security risks associated with wireless communication systems that use dual hop OFDM technology. To mitigate this issue, we analyze two main cases: one involving a single user with a single relay, and another with multiple users and relays. The primary goal of this investigation is to determine optimal power allocation methods across various frequencies in order to enhance end-to-end data transmission security while adhering to power consumption constraints at both the sender and relay nodes. Text-based games provide a rigorous platform to assess virtual agents in tasks like natural language understanding, solving complex problems, and applying real-world knowledge.
One significant limitation of existing text-based games lies in their slow speed, topping out at around 300 actions per second, largely because of outdated technology used to create them.
Our research presents TextWorldExpress, a highly optimized version of three widely used text-based game challenges, achieving a remarkable increase in simulation processing speed of roughly three orders of magnitude.
On ordinary computer hardware, it can process over one million actions per second, allowing for extensive tests lasting merely a day rather than weeks or even months. We demonstrate that intense testing requires incredibly high simulation processing power, surpassing the speed required to generate accurate predictions from modern artificial intelligence models by a significant margin. Nonetheless, we found that TextWorldExpress enables fast testing of virtual agents and helps identify certain optimization strategies that significantly reduce the time needed to test agent performance by a factor of ten. Our research implies that text-based games must be continually evolved to keep pace with the rapid development of artificial intelligence technology. Our data and methods are available for public use at https://textworldexpress.github.io/. Our hope is that this initiative encourages more researchers to engage with text-based games in the future. Our team intends to expand the framework to accommodate an even broader range of existing text-based games challenges. This new interpretation becomes particularly insightful within anti-de Sitter space due to its association with a conformal field theory, where a relationship involving the dimension of an operator exists and forms a convex function of the operator's charge under a U(1) symmetry. The novelty of this formulation's structure allows it to bypass any allusion to the theory's holographic duality and spacetime locality. Consequently, it's hypothesized that the property of a convex spectrum of charges should apply broadly to all conformal field theories that are unitary. The rapid transformation of the electricity sector necessitates innovative ancillary services that guarantee the stability and dependability of the electricity network. Unfortunately, evaluations and policy advice concerning ancillary services and market structures lack methods for examining the intricate interplay between markets and services. Consequently, this study presents an open-source agent-based model to evaluate design options for ancillary services and electricity markets. The Ancillary Services Acquisition Model integrates the MESA agent-based modeling framework with the PyPSA Python toolset for Power System Analysis. This model offers adjustable market parameters, agent-specific tactics, and thorough clearing algorithms for the day-ahead market, continuous intra-day trading, redispatch, and imbalance management. Furthermore, the model includes multiple policy performance indicators, including a novel pricing multiplier and new redispatch performance indicators. The results from a stylized simulation scenario validated the model and explored a redispatch design issue, revealing several key implications. The findings indicate that, when implementing order types in multi-period redispatch markets, the following effects are produced: the risk is minimized for market participants due to complete order fulfillment, but this may lead to increased trading of imbalances during intra-day and dispatch ramp risks, resulting from large orders; meanwhile, the grid operator over-procures redispatch during peak periods when all-or-none design is employed, which can also lead to induced imbalances due to inadequate redispatch activation. Nonetheless, the impact of these consequences on the durability and dependability of the electricity system remains subject to evaluation through further research utilizing the Ancillary Services Acquisition Model. The model is accessible at https://github.com/enerthink/ancillary-services-acquisition-model. The corresponding PyPSA-SHADE code is available at https://github.com/pypsa/pypsa-shade. The model and PyPSA-SHADE can be downloaded from the above links or accessed via the following DOIs: Ancillary Services Acquisition Model: https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/3GQ8CG, PyPSA-SHADE: https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/3GQ8DH. The data used to demonstrate the model are publicly available at https://github.com/enerthink/ancillary-services-acquisition-model-data. The approach presented in this study can be applied to recent design frameworks for markets and ancillary services in Europe, such as the market design for the electricity market union, the approach is also applicable to other global markets, such as the organized electricity markets in the United States, Australia, and New Zealand.

R.W.K. Odoni initially established the connection between the Galois group of an iterated polynomial and the symmetric group in fields of characteristic zero. A generalization to fields of positive characteristic was achieved by Juul. Building on these findings, we explore a scenario involving an irreducible polynomial F over the algebraic closure of a finite field k(t) with algebraic and separable coefficients. When a generic monic polynomial Phi is composed with F, resulting in a new polynomial with coefficients (a0, a1,...), we identify the Galois group of the composite polynomial's mth iterate. The structure of this Galois group mirrors the (m-folded) iterated wreath product of the symmetric group S_(nd) for n > 0, where n represents the polynomial's degree. In the case of large finite fields, the application of this discovery aligns with analogous theories, including the polynomial equivalent of the Bateman-Horn conjecture, the Chowla's conjecture regarding autocorrelation, and the Chebotarev density theorem over function fields. Additionally, this research supplements the polynomial analogue of the Riemann hypothesis, known as the Weil conjectures. It also extends the recent work of Jones on the random matrix theory equivalent of the pair correlation of zeros of L-functions in the complex plane. By connecting the Galois group of the mth iterate of a generic polynomial of degree d > 0 to the symmetric group, we establish a connection between the mth iterate of these polynomials and the minimal confounding family of polynomials, which consists of the irreducible, monic polynomials with coefficients in the algebraic closure of a finite field k(t) and coefficient degrees defined by the symmetric group S_(md) for m > 0. This connection further establishes the equivalence of two events: the event that the mth iterate of these polynomials corresponds to the symmetric group S_(nd) and the event that the minimal confounding family is defined by the symmetric group S_(md) for m > 0. Saturn's polar atmosphere is characterized by seasonal variations of large warm whirlpools north of 75 degrees latitude. The strongest of these appear during Saturn's summer and disappear in the winter. The extensive exploration of the Saturn system enabled by the Cassini spacecraft has facilitated a comprehensive study of the formation of the North Polar Stratospheric Vortex through the application of infrared spectroscopy. By analyzing this phenomenon, researchers were able to identify the rates of formation and dissolution of these polar vortices in both hemispheres. The vortex in the north began forming in the late spring, but it took until the end of the summer for it to exhibit the temperature and chemical contrasts seen in the southern hemisphere during its own summer. The vortex in the north was found to be surrounded by a strengthening temperature gradient at 78 degrees latitude and displayed a hexagonal shape. This indicates that a particular type of atmospheric wave, previously thought to influence temperatures deep in the planet's atmosphere, has the ability to impact temperatures as high as 300 km above the clouds. The reduction in the strength of this wave during the summer leads to a decrease in the outside temperature and an increase in the altitude of the polar atmosphere, which in turn leads to the formation of these warm vortices. The research on the southern hemisphere revealed a significant increase in the altitude of the polar atmosphere in the late autumn, which resulted in the disappearance of the southern vortex and the return of the particular type of atmospheric wave to its previous strength. This caused a return to the conditions that formed the warm vortices in the north. The study of the southern hemisphere also showed that the temperature and chemical contrasts in the polar vortex in the south remained strong through the entire winter, unlike the vortex in the north. This difference is believed to be influenced by the different amounts of sunlight the two hemispheres receive during their respective winters. The interaction between the polar vortex and the stratospheric circulation in the equatorial regions of the Saturn system was also examined. The application of a new analytical technique enabled by the high-resolution data from the Cassini spacecraft revealed the presence of a particular type of wave that was circulating around the planet and was affecting the temperature and chemical composition of the upper atmosphere. This wave was found to be responsible for the distribution of chemicals in the polar vortex in the north and the sudden drops in temperature in the equatorial regions during the spring and the autumn. The interaction between the polar vortex and the equatorial regions of the Saturn system also facilitated the study of the circulation in the stratospheric regions

The interaction between light and matter is used in various spectroscopic techniques to extract details about a sample's molecular, atomic, or nuclear components. Although scattered light conveys both amplitude and phase information, this phase information is frequently lost during standard intensity measurements, yet it is crucial for reconstructing essential details of a target, as evident from applications like coherent x-ray imaging. A new algorithm is introduced that allows for retrieving phase information from two-dimensional time- and energy-resolved spectra, a feature we demonstrate with x-ray scattering off M\"ossbauer nuclei using a synchrotron radiation source. The knowledge gained through phase information also leads to accurate reconstruction of energy spectra from experimental data, a level of precision that cannot be achieved with other methods. Our approach provides a useful data analysis tool, offering a beneficial impact on x-ray quantum optics and M\"ossbauer spectroscopy that employs synchrotron radiation. Additionally, this method has the potential to be implemented on other x-ray sources, such as x-ray generators used in M\"ossbauer spectroscopy, and other experimental configurations that involve x-rays and scattered light, with both time and energy resolution. The development of this algorithm was motivated by M\"ossbauer spectroscopy, a technique that can be enhanced by x-ray phase information, yet current limitations result in the rejection of half of the available scattering events due to time-domain interference, a problem that this research aims to address by recovering the necessary information from the recorded spectra. By obtaining phase information and reconstructing scattered spectra from the time and energy domains, we have achieved a 2.3 times improvement in data completeness when using a 12Si semiconductor detector at a synchrotron radiation source, with 10 MHz count rates and a minimum energy threshold of 6 keV, for the measurement of $^{57}$Fe decay energies. This breakthrough leads to a 40 times improvement in data completeness for energies below 10 keV, within the same count rate and duration, further highlighting the value of retaining phase information in x-ray scattering off nuclei using a synchrotron radiation source. The developed algorithm has been made available through the xMOSsim package, an extension for the MOSsim software that models and analyzes x-ray M\"ossbauer spectroscopy data involving scattered light and includes both time and energy resolution. The algorithm's effectiveness is demonstrated on realistic experimental data sets. The code and data used for the analysis are accessible via the xMOSsim website. Hypothesis evaluation plays a significant role in cognitive science, where Bayes factors can compare and contrast competing theories by assessing their consistency with available data. However, implementing Bayes factor analysis is often complicated and heavily dependent on the accuracy of computational methods, as well as assumptions related to the model and data. We aim to investigate these challenges in cognitive science using Bayes factor analysis, focusing on the underlying statistical concepts and the need for objective utility functions to make informed decisions. We explore various issues with Bayes factor estimates, including their tendency to err and the reliability of bridge sampling, especially when analyzing complex scenarios. To tackle these challenges, we develop a simulation-based approach for validating the accuracy of Bayes factor estimates and examine the stability of Bayes factors in relation to different Markov chain Monte Carlo (MCMC) draws. We also investigate the variability of Bayes factor estimates and the effectiveness of utility functions in making informed decisions. To facilitate the assessment of Bayes factor reliability, we outline a step-by-step workflow that researchers can use to evaluate the performance of Bayes factor analysis for their individual studies, including an illustrative example from the cognitive sciences. We anticipate that this research will contribute to the development of a robust methodology for evaluating scientific hypotheses based on Bayes factor analysis, along with reproducible code available online. To improve the effectiveness of sentence representations in classification tasks, research has been done on predicting these indicators between sentences. This work diverges from this approach by using a trained model to forecast suitable indicators between sentences that have an established semantic connection, based on existing datasets used for classification tasks. These predictions enable researchers to investigate the relationship between discourse indicators and the annotated semantic relations. Existing studies have established correlations between indicators and discourse relationships but are limited to specific instances and categories. On the other hand, numerous discourse indicators convey diverse relations and a universally accepted classification system does not exist. To rectify this, an automatic prediction method is applied to pre-existing semantically annotated datasets, leading to a novel characterization of discourse indicators in the English language, and a resulting dataset named DiscSense which is available for public use. Evaluations based on classification accuracy show that the predicted discourse indicators correlate strongly with the existing annotations, despite the lack of a standardized classification framework. Nonetheless, the characterization of discourse indicators does not depend on the specific classification system, rather it is centered on the underlying semantic connections they convey. Furthermore, a comparison with a manually annotated dataset named DiscStruct, reveals an interesting contrast in the predicted discourse indicators, revealing an underlying structure that has not been previously identified, thereby validating the utility of the approach. Ultimately, this research demonstrates the utility of predicting discourse indicators when exploring the underlying connections between sentences, and the novelty of the resulting characterization of discourse indicators can be applied to various English sentence datasets. The theoretical foundation of the research is based on the notion that the semantic connections between sentences are discourse-dependent, as exemplified by the contrast between the connections in the following examples: "Sushi is expensive." -- "Sushi isn't expensive." as opposed to "Sushi is delicious." -- "Sushi isn't delicious." Where the connection between the two sentences about the price of sushi is one of contrast, whereas the connection between the two sentences about the taste of sushi is one of opposition. This demonstrates that the same two sentences can have different discourse dependencies and consequently different semantic connections between them. Consequently, to understand the meaning of individual sentences, it is necessary to consider the surrounding sentences and the discourse dependencies between them. The most suitable discourse indicators for describing the connection between the two sentences about the taste of sushi would be "by contrast", whereas the most suitable indicator for the two sentences about the price of sushi would be "on the contrary".
