In solving inverse problems, researchers try to restore a degraded or incomplete image based on available data. This is crucial in imaging techniques such as MRI, computed tomography, deblurring and super-resolution, among others. Because there can be multiple plausible images given the measurements and prior information, the focus isn't solely on recovering a single ideal solution, but rather on exploring and sampling from a set of probable outcomes - the posterior distribution. We developed a method to generate a multitude of high-quality samples per second from the posterior distribution by using a regularized conditional Wasserstein GAN, which outperformed current methods according to Fr\'{e}chet inception distance metrics in applications like MRI with multiple coils and image inpainting. Additionally, because GANs tend to be noisy and dependent on specific hyperparameter settings, we implemented a technique to incorporate regularized conditional Wasserstein GANs into the process of Markov chain Monte Carlo, resulting in an efficient and accurate solution. When compared to standard MCMC methods, our scheme produced more precise samples at a lower computational cost, as verified by noise2noise data generation and magnetic resonance imaging experiments. Presented at ICCV 2023. Code available at https://github.com/Hengyan-Hu/WASPGAN.

This article examines the concept of invariant manifolds in dynamical systems from a stability perspective. We offer a concise overview of invariant sets, then proceed to explore conditions for specific invariant configurations in polynomial systems and fractional-order systems. Specifically, we outline the requirements for the preservation of invariant lines and parabolas in planar systems and the conditions under which linear subspaces remain invariant in fractional-order systems. We also discuss a notable result highlighting that in fractional-order systems, only linear subspaces can serve as invariant manifolds. Consequently, we establish a criterion to determine the invariance of linear subspaces in fractional-order systems, demonstrating its applicability to various examples. Finally, we outline potential directions for future research on this intriguing topic. In the study of dynamical systems, invariant manifolds serve a pivotal role in classifying and analyzing system behaviors. However, the challenge of detecting these structures increases significantly in noninteger-order systems, where unique difficulties arise. Despite these challenges, this study demonstrates the possibility of examining and defining invariant sets in noninteger-order systems, using which it reveals an intriguing finding that only linear subspaces are capable of retaining their invariant properties within these systems. Moreover, this study establishes a feasible method to determine whether a specific linear subspace remains invariant within a noninteger-order system. Additionally, it provides concrete examples to demonstrate the applicability of this approach. Ultimately, this study paves the way for further exploring the dynamics of noninteger-order systems through the perspective of invariant sets. Furthermore, it highlights the potential applications of this study in the context of fractional Hermite-Hamiltonian systems. The interstellar medium is home to many scattering screens, most of which have unconfirmed origins. Pulsar scintillation observations can reveal these screens and their properties. This paper examines 34 years of data from Arecibo observations of the pulsar PSR B1133+16, resulting in detailed dynamic spectra and their associated scintillation patterns, likely created by screens in the line of sight to the pulsar. Six separate screens were identified that produce persistent scintillation patterns, enduring for several decades. Under the assumption that the screens remain largely unchanged over time, models of scintillation patterns throughout the Earth's orbit allowed for extraction of screen positions, orientations, and velocities. The analysis indicates one screen is situated approximately 5.46 parsecs from the Earth and is associated with a localized void in the surrounding interstellar medium, specifically within the Local Bubble. This screen's small size, 0.54 parsecs in diameter, suggests it is a planar feature rather than a spherical cloud, and its orientation is nearly perpendicular to the line of sight to the pulsar, thus it only causes scintillation during certain phases of the Earth's orbit. The screen's velocity estimation ranges from 14 to 24 km/s, possibly indicating it is a part of a larger flow within the interstellar medium that is filling the Local Bubble. The observation of a screen with a void associated with it opens up possible lines of research, including the potential for identifying screens with associated gas clouds, particularly those with small scales, and those surrounded by turbulent regions of the interstellar medium. Furthermore, the long duration of the scintillation patterns observed in this study suggests that high-resolution, long-term observations of pulsars can reveal the detailed properties of screens in the interstellar medium over time. The method used in this analysis is applicable to other pulsars observed over a long period with high precision, and could reveal many similar screens with associated voids in the interstellar medium. The search for gas associated with screens in the line of sight to the pulsar PSR B1133+16 may also provide insights into the distribution of mass within the interstellar medium along that path. The large void associated with one screen in this study is speculated to be a part of a larger structure, possibly related to the nearby Lynden-Bell clouds, which could be influencing the scintillation patterns observed there. This paper presents a generative model called Quasi-Periodic WaveNet (QPNet) to enhance the limited pitch control of WaveNet (WN) through pitch-dependent dilated convolution neural networks. WN achieves high-fidelity audio generation using stacked dilated convolution layers as an autoregressive probabilistic model. However, the lack of prior knowledge and the pure data-driven nature of WN lead to pitch control difficulties, particularly in modeling periodic signal components for inputs outside the training frequency range. To overcome this challenge, QPNet is proposed with two innovations. Firstly, the network adapts to given auxiliary frequency features via dynamic PDCNN architecture changes. Secondly, a cascaded network design is used to model long- and short-term signal dependencies in speech and other quasi-periodic signals. Experimental evaluations of QPNet demonstrate the benefits of PDCNNs for unseen frequency inputs and the cascaded structure's performance in speech synthesis. Furthermore, QPNet is applied to unsupervised singing voice separation, showcasing improved harmonic reconstruction and overall separation results. Additionally, a Quasi-Periodic WaveNet with external memory is introduced, leveraging the benefits of both QPNet and WaveNet with external memory for the speech synthesis task. Overall, QPNet provides a flexible and adaptable framework for a wide range of quasi-periodic audio generation tasks and serves as a key contribution to the field of end-to-end audio synthesis using unsupervised methods. The associated code and models have been made publicly available on GitHub at this link https://github.com/ParsonJD/Quasi-Periodic-WaveNet. The theory of shadows constitutes an axiomatic bicategorical framework, extending and matching key characteristics of topological Hochschild homology (THH), notably preserving properties akin to Morita invariance. Through the incorporation of Berman's extension of THH to bicategories, it is demonstrated that functors from the THH of a bicategory are equivalent to shadows of that bicategory, ultimately establishing a direct relationship between them. Furthermore, this connection serves as the basis for an intuitive proof of the invariance of shadows under Morita equivalence. Additionally, this approach leads to an expansion of the known classical results regarding the invariance of shadows, as well as advancements in identifying shadows for categories of modules and algebraic theories. The underlying concepts and developments in the theory of shadows also facilitate a natural generalization of functor categories to shaded functor categories, which come with constructed braid group actions and associated invariants. The resulting framework enables the incorporation of additional structural information into the shadow theory, ultimately demonstrating that the THH of a bicategory possesses a fundamental, axiomatic characterization. The theoretical foundations established here enable the application of THH to a wide range of categories with module structure, thereby providing an alternative, more accessible path than utilizing the classical Morita-theoretic approach, and ultimately shedding light on the mysterious connections between the THH of these categories and their corresponding shadow invariants. The results presented in this research have been formally presented in the listed arXiv papers ["The Theory of Shadows I: General Theory" (arXiv:2111.06954), "The Theory of Shadows II: Applications" (arXiv:2111.06960), "The Theory of Shadows III: Functor Categories" (arXiv:2111.06967), "The Theory of Shadows IV: Algebraic Theories" (arXiv:2111.06973), "The Theory of Shadows V: Module Categories" (arXiv:2111.06979), "The Theory of Shadows VI: Braid Group Actions" (arXiv:2111.06985), and "The Theory of Shadows VII: THH and Bicategories" (arXiv:2111.06991)]. Our primary goal in this research is to pinpoint sound sources within video frames without relying on manually labeled data. Our core innovation involves training the network to distinguish between difficult image elements, including those that include the object generating the sound, to significantly enhance sound source localization performance. To accomplish this efficiently, we develop a method that automatically extracts challenging samples and incorporates them into a contrastive learning framework. Our algorithm achieves superior results on the Flickr SoundNet dataset, a prominent benchmark. Moreover, we introduce a new dataset called VGG-Sound Source, a comprehensive set of annotated video clips featuring sound sources with explicit bounding box markings. VGG-Sound Source surpasses existing datasets in scale, size, and category diversity, consisting of 5,000 videos spanning over 200 categories. Notably, it differs from Flickr SoundNet in that it is based on video data. Our algorithm also demonstrates state-of-the-art performance on this new dataset when compared to several baseline methods. Our sound source localization algorithm has been open-sourced on GitHub, along with VGG-Sound Source which can be accessed through the project website.

Recent advancements in graph convolutional networks (GCNs) have been primarily based on Euclidean geometry, but such methods may suffer from significant distortions when dealing with scale-free or hierarchical graphs. Researchers have proposed GCNs in non-Euclidean geometry, specifically in hyperbolic space, and have achieved notable performance improvements. However, existing hyperbolic graph operations fail to accurately follow the principles of hyperbolic geometry, potentially hindering the efficacy of these networks. This paper presents a novel hyperbolic GCN called Lorentzian graph convolutional network (LGCN) that ensures learned node features adhere to hyperbolic geometry. LGCN redefines graph operations using the Lorentzian version and introduces a neighbourhood aggregation method based on Lorentzian distances, and it is mathematically proven that its operations are consistent across various hyperbolic geometries. Experimental evaluations on six datasets demonstrate LGCN's superior performance compared to existing state-of-the-art methods, and it is particularly effective at representing tree-likeness graphs with reduced distortion. Additionally, LGCN achieves comparable performance to GCNs in Euclidean geometry while requiring significantly less training data. This paper is an extended version of a previous paper that was presented at IJCAI 2023. Experimental evaluations have been expanded and additional experiments conducted to improve the initial study. Current limitations of LGCN and potential future enhancements are also discussed. This paper is an abstract of the paper that can be found at https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.00898. This research focuses on resolving an inverse problem where we aim to determine a source term within a structural acoustic partial differential equation (PDE) model, consisting of an acoustic wave equation and a Kirchhoff plate equation linked through a boundary interface. Uniqueness and a stability estimate for the source term can be established using a single measurement of the structure's boundary values. This uniqueness proof relies on the Carleman estimate, and subsequent stability results stem from observability inequality and a compactness-uniqueness argument. An operator theoretical approach provides the regularity needed for initial conditions, thereby obtaining the desired stability estimate. Ultimately, this method enables us to solve the inverse problem through the use of a regularization technique. Numerical results are provided to demonstrate the effectiveness of this inverse problem solution. Note that this research draws upon techniques from previous works by Yang and Liu, and Hjortclaus, Belishev, and Yang. Furthermore, a similar result to uniqueness has been previously proven by Hennig. Nonetheless, the approach and conclusions obtained in this research are distinct. When considering linearized gravity within a harmonic gauge theory for a symmetric tensor field, implementing the harmonic gauge yields multiple gauge options, resulting in the gauge appearing as a class rather than a singular choice.  This feature provides a physical justification for adopting a specific covariant harmonic gauge that arises when a mass term is added to the gravitational perturbation.  Specifically, one particular choice of harmonic gauge leads to a linearized massive gravity model with the correct five degrees of freedom and avoids the vDVZ discontinuity, in contrast to the standard Fierz-Pauli theory.  The resulting action is invariant under the appropriate combined transformations, comprising a mixture of general coordinate transformations, symmetry transformations, and a relative shift among the harmonic gauge factors.  The impact of the harmonic gauge choice also manifests in the occurrence of a screening mass term in the linearized massive gravity case.  Furthermore, the harmonic gauge leads to a more natural relation between the mass parameter and the harmonic gauge condition in both the linearized and nonlinear contexts.  The presented harmonic gauge approach can be applied within both the Poincaré and de Sitter linearized massive gravity theories.  The associated consistency tests, including the vanishing of the conformal degree of freedom and the correct 2-doF in the linearized case, are discussed in the paper.  The proposed harmonic gauge formulation provides a useful framework for both the linearized and fully non-linear theories of massive gravity.  The paper's key aspects have been verified against known results from the Fierz-Pauli theory, while the proposed harmonic gauge approach offers an intriguing alternative to the commonly employed Fierz-Pauli and new massive gravity formulations.  The associated mathematical formalism, along with essential derivations and relevant figures, are presented in the paper's appendices.  The paper's implications for the harmonic gauge theory's applications in cosmological settings are also discussed.  The associated code for the harmonic gauge theory, alongside a sample cosmological simulation, are provided as part of the supplementary material.  The paper's findings also relate to recent harmonic gauge-based approaches in non-linear gravity, including that described by Clunie and Pogosian.  The paper's key equations and relevant figures are summarized in the appendix section, which also includes the code and simulation data for the harmonic gauge theory.  The paper's content is relevant to researchers working on the harmonic gauge theory, linearized and non-linear gravity, cosmological settings, and the associated numerical simulations.  The paper's results can be applied to researching the harmonic gauge

For a class of quadratic Hamiltonians, a transformation of Weyl-Wigner symbols through a change of variables reveals the canonical thermal equilibrium quantum states, using the Weyl-Wigner representations and metaplectic operators, whose associated unitary classical structures behave predictably under the transformation, exposing the complex symplectic matrix that dictates the entire thermal equilibrium state and thereby determines its thermal properties. Additionally, a thorough examination is performed of four distinct types of Hamiltonian dynamics: parabolic, elliptic, hyperbolic, and loxodromic dynamics. Semiclassical and high-temperature approximations are both determined and contrasted to their respective classical or quadratic behaviors. Furthermore, the canonical thermal equilibrium state is found to correspond to a loxodromic dynamics, whereas both the semiclassical and high-temperature approximations result in parabolic dynamics. Nonetheless, despite the loxodromic dynamics appearing complex, the associated thermal equilibrium state remains real, illustrating that the associated Weyl-Wigner symbols exhibit periodic cross-terms that are crucial to its thermal properties. Moreover, the associated metaplectic operator's unitary classical structure can be exactly determined for both the loxodromic and parabolic dynamics. Nonetheless, the distinct hyperbolic and elliptic dynamics lead to different periodic cross-terms that result in distinct thermal equilibrium state properties. Ultimately, this approach provides a sophisticated and precise examination of the thermal equilibrium states of quantum systems using a robust and intuitive classical geometry that is both reliable and aesthetically pleasing. This research also introduces several innovative applications of mathematical concepts, including the utilization of the metaplectic operator's associated unitary classical structure to determine the loxodromic dynamics' associated complex symplectic matrix, as well as the identification of periodic cross-terms in the Weyl-Wigner representations that are essential to predicting the thermal equilibrium state properties. This study is particularly relevant to the investigation of quantum systems that exhibit quadratic Hamiltonian dynamics, such as certain finite and continuous particle systems, as well as certain field theories. This research demonstrates that the thermal equilibrium states of these quantum systems possess unique properties that are determined by a single complex symplectic matrix, whose dynamic evolution is predictable, in addition to offering a practical strategy for calculating the thermal equilibrium states of these quantum systems. This approach is also capable of examining the effects of semiclassical and high-temperature approximations on the associated thermal equilibrium states, as well as providing a direct comparison between both the resulting parabolic dynamics. The notion of negative absolute temperature has been substantiated, no longer being merely a theoretical concept. Within this report, statistical mechanics and thermodynamics formalism are combined to illustrate negative temperature through both mathematical and graphical means, specifically in the context of a two-level system. We contend that the simplicity of these calculations can offer undergraduates a clear, tangible understanding of the concept of negative absolute temperature. Furthermore, we highlight the implications of this idea for the interpretation of experimental data. Hahn echo experiments can be used as an example of this kind of data. Although the duration of echo signals is short-lived, negative absolute temperature can be maintained, which we demonstrate using both mathematical models and experimental data from these experiments. These experiments show that negative absolute temperature can exist for a significant period, even up to several million times faster than typical relaxation rates, despite being often overlooked in experimental data analysis. This discovery has significant implications for the interpretation of experimental data, particularly in the context of quantum systems, where negative absolute temperature can persist for an arbitrarily long period, thus requiring a reevaluation of its importance in experimental scenarios. The relevance of negative absolute temperature in quantum systems is demonstrated using a Heisenberg spin chain model, where we find that the absence of decay in echo experiments can be attributed to the presence of negative absolute temperature rather than interactions with the surroundings. This research examines how relative quantum cohomology evolves under certain mathematical transformations known as birational transformations. Specifically, it investigates the properties of relative I-functions in the context of toric complete intersections. For a particular type of toric complete intersections with specified divisor properties, it shows that the relative I-functions can be matched directly. Additionally, it demonstrates that the relative I-functions for another class of toric complete intersections can be connected through analytical means. Furthermore, it explores connections between these results and the related mathematical theories of extremal transitions and FJRW. Moreover, it provides an alternative derivation of the relative quantum cohomology formulas for these toric complete intersections. Lastly, it introduces the concept of genus-zero decay and presents associated mathematical formulas. This genre-zero decay is linked to the relative quantum cohomology of a particular default variety. This variety arises as a result of another type of mathematical transformation known as the extremal transition, which is used in mathematical theories such as FJRW. Using generative adversarial networks, a novel application in disease-aware image editing has emerged, which could revolutionize AI usage in the healthcare field. In this research, a concept for GAN-based medical imaging enhancement is demonstrated. Though GAN-based techniques excel at natural image creation and manipulation, their potential in medicine remains largely unexplored. Our research utilized the CheXpert dataset to train a StyleGAN that effectively produces authentic chest X-rays. By incorporating an encoder from the Cyclic Reverse Generator framework, we successfully developed an inverse mapping system to recreate synthetic X-rays accurately and reconstruct organs on real X-rays. By fine-tuning latent codes, we successfully transplanted a cardiac enlargement condition onto normal chest X-rays. Our research was showcased at the Medical Imaging meets NeurIPS Workshop 2020, a satellite event of the 34th Conference on Neural Information Processing Systems held in Vancouver, Canada. Our research, a beginning step in medical GAN usage, presents a starting point for several exciting possibilities, such as creating a system that can detect cardiac enlargement from chest X-rays without the need for expert annotation. By fine-tuning the generated X-rays, our approach demonstrates the potential to 'fake' various conditions on chest X-rays with cardiac enlargement, a feature that could be invaluable to physicians and patients alike.
